item.description:
We're still about six months out from the release of Final Fantasy 7 Revelation, the final part of the FF7 Remake trilogy. But, already, there is a lot of discussion about the size of the game; whether it's all the divisive side activities on offer in the title, or the fact it won't be shipping totally on-disc at launch thanks to the amount of stuff it'll feature, director Naoki Hamaguchi is already fielding a lot of questions about 'size versus quality' in the last game in the Remake series.
In a new interview with VGC, the outspoken director notes that he's "not worried about the scale". He goes on to explain that the reason the game can't ship on disc (or even two discs, like Rebirth did) is because he's expecting the file size to be absolutely massive.
"Things are still getting worked out, but it’s probably going to be around 200GB of game," he says to VGC. "I understand there are a lot of opinions about this topic, but at the end of the day, the fact is we need to overcome the hardware to a certain extent."
Rebirth weighs in at 91GB on Switch 2, 145GB on PS5, 169GB on Xbox Series, and 155GB on PC, so depending on format, Revelation looks set to be up to twice as large as the last game in the series. Woof. The game will also receive two bonus DLC packages post-launch, and these will be similar in size to Remake's Intermission DLC, per Hamaguchi. "It's best to imagine the DLC like what we did with Intermission: digging deeper into the characters of Vincent and Sephiroth. In regard to whether those stories take place in the past or the present, I’m not going to tell you that now, but we’re excited to reveal that."
As the sort of sicko that routinely goes over 100 hours for my RPG reviews, I must say this both excites and terrifies me. For consumers, I have seen a lot of discussion this week about game length, thanks to the previously-linked Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave review - it seems, understandably, that games with a runtime of over 100 hours are simply too demanding for many adults with lives, jobs, and responsibilities to consider.
Final Fantasy 7 Revelation launches 8th April, 2027 for Xbox Series X/S, PlayStation 5, PC, and Nintendo Switch 2, and I'm curious to see if the trilogy will be able to stick the landing, or whether the whole thing will crumble under the weight of all this open world ambition. I've spoken to Hamaguchi about this before, and his answers to my concerns about open world game design put my mind at ease, at least.

item.description:
The first time I ate mold was like something out of a Victorian morality play. It was in boarding school, when fuzzy blue-grey discs would sometimes appear on the bottom of a quiche, or after I saw one of the kitchen ladies use a cleaning rag to cover a tray of cauliflower cheese. We were told it was a good source of protein, and because I complained, I had to collect rubbish for a weekend in my school uniform. Outside the realm of edible mushrooms and respectable fungi and polite society, the idea of eating mold is kinda gross. But here I am, in Control Resonant, faced with the Temptation of Saint Mycology, while my handler screams in my ear for me to put the mold down. I will not. I'm Dylan Faden, and this is Jackass.
Dylan, who became an indentured lab rat at age ten, never got to watch Jackass, because up until five minutes ago he was in a coma, and before that, he was possessed by a malevolent entity called the Hiss. His AWOL sister Jesse, the Director of the Federal Bureau of Control, oversaw a seven-year lockdown to contain the Hiss in the Oldest House after the events of the first game; in the present, the Hiss escapes into Manhattan and everything hits the proverbial fan. Dylan must help the Bureau deal with a new threat as the city is cut off from the outside world, while also searching for Jesse, who may not even be on the same dimensional plane.
I loved Control. I have fond memories of exploring New York and learning how bad the city smells after a spring rain. I love over-the-top paratextual worldbuilding and the X-Files and goofy nods to new weird literary themes. The best part of Control was how well it mythologised a vast and indifferent bureaucracy, thanks largely to the SCP Foundation, a collaborative online fiction project that Remedy drew on for inspiration, and how that arcane mythology imprinted so perfectly on a whole administration of dyed-in-the-wool civil servants and 1960s-era pneumatic tubes. Hell hath no petty like a disgruntled worker filing HR complaints while a hivemind takes over the building, and together, all of the game's documents and recordings and found items told a banger piece of speculative fiction that vibrated on the same dysfunctional frequency as the House. The tonal contrast of bland mundanity and eldritch freakshow isn't a new combo, but it works really well for a reason, and it was a huge part of what gave Control the juice.
Remedy has since described each Control game as a reflection of each respective Faden protagonist. Unfortunately this makes Control the tighter and more narratively cohesive sibling, while Control Resonant is kind of all over the place. Big sister was a game that understood the genres it drew from, and most importantly, knew what it wasn't (the combat systems weren't very good then, and they're still not great now, but let's be real – no one is playing Remedy games for the combat). Little brother, though, feels pulled in different directions, and follows a more emotional path as it gets deeper into family dynamics, few of which are particularly striking, and, with a couple of exceptions, don't add much to the story that 1) you can't infer yourself and 2) wouldn't be better off left in the periphery of the player's imagination.
Control Resonant is by necessity a different creature from Control. For starters, it's much more of a triple-A-flavoured action RPG, with a big wide map of tiny little markers for everything from persons of interest and repeating world events. There's a discernible loss of focus now that we're outside the Oldest House, whose shifting architecture was a core part of how Control cultivated and maintained such an effective atmosphere. The Oldest House was a moody, ancient Brutalist cocoon full of secrets – you couldn't trust the walls around you, which was a neat setting for getting sucked into the bowels of a government agency. Dylan is a maladapted sadboy experiencing the real world for the first time as an adult, and to this end, a big overwhelming city makes sense to tell this type of story. Manhattan fragmented and literally turned upside-down because of reality-changing interdimensional physics – there is at least one Inception joke in the game – feels appropriate for a guy who just came out of a coma, but it also means all that smartly-styled weirdness gets diluted into Marvel-style blockbuster flatness. There's just about no suspense left when you can climb onto a rooftop, look out, and see all the areas brewing with Hiss or Mold.
Accordingly, the open-ended world (Remedy is keen to remind us this is, technically, not an open world) lends itself much more to an FBC team-building group-effort situation – Dylan's handler, agent Zoe de Vera, plays the straight man buffer between Dylan and the bureau and tries to make peace with her own role in an organisation that made his life hell. World events involve supporting FBC rangers in the field (defend the cargo, protect the worker, and so on) and after a certain point Dylan unlocks a chore board for garden-variety escort missions and fetch quests. He meets different factions within the bureau (shoutout to the mold people and Langston) as he tries to prove that he isn't a homicidal meat puppet anymore. There's the usual triple-A dance between big save-the-world story beats and minor side stories where all the best writing is hidden, but at times, like when Zoe radios Dylan to do nothingburger tasks after a big urgent plot reveal, the pacing suffers. The cumulative effect is a kind of narrative sprawl, an inversion of the purpose that shaped Jesse's journey in Control. I should know something about how turgid and dull main questlines are: I play Final Fantasy 14.
Combat-wise, Dylan is a melee guy. His main abilities are straightforward button-spammers with a sprinkling of tactical support skills; new combat abilities are learned by defeating bosses called Resonants. His weapon is the Aberrant, essentially a paranatural metal bar that can morph into whatever the moment needs (it also houses a familiar friend from the first game). In line with Remedy's action-RPG aspirations, they've refined skill trees to hew closer to familiar class conventions, so players can choose a high-crit build or focus on crowd control and AOE attacks. I use Glaive as my primary ability – it gives the Aberrant a big swing with a knockback – and start golfing my way through mobs. It does not feel as meaty as I would like it to, and this is certainly not Dynasty Warriors, but I eventually find joy in a secondary fire punch skill that is exceptionally powerful against Mold. Inquiring minds will want to know if Control's combat has improved, and the unfortunate answer is not really.
Traversal abilities are learned from Faults, which are sort of interdimensional "thin" places where Dylan senses Jesse. Faults offer interactive storytime and explore the Fadens' link as siblings united by trauma, which in turn involves a lot of repetitive leaping and dashing paired with childhood dysfunction. Most of this is Mike Flanagan-level melodramatic, and I am not a fan of what Mike Flanagan has done to horror and the way it intersects so limply with therapy and trauma.
Because this is Remedy, the game hammers home its hyper-meta themes of refraction and recursion at every possible opportunity, so I am, to an extent, prepared to get lost and do things over and over again. But when the gravity mechanics kick in and Dylan has to move between planes on a timer, navigating becomes trickier and puzzles become a little more involved, and when you throw in a mess of dynamic markers and deliberately disorienting gameplay, some of which demand falling from a great height on a precise trajectory, hitting a nice flow can get frustrating (there were also a couple times when my Inception shenanigans got me stuck in a chasm behind a wall).
Is messing with gravity cool? Did you like Gravity Rush? Yes, walking up walls is always cool, but a lot of the "Dylan swooping around New York" stuff plays out like Spider-Man helping literal puppies and saving civilians. Frankly, I could do routine superheroing in a better action game – this is not why I want to play a Control game.
As a result, Control Resonant doesn't truly hit its stride until Dylan is beneath the Oldest House in the Underpass. Here, my second-favorite story arc unfolds through reports and recordings – an understated cosmic horror workplace drama podcast, set against a backdrop of monolithic office columns and minimalist Zdzisław Beksiński landscape vibes (there is also an Interstellar-inspired questline in the adjacent area, which feels like one too many Nolans for a single meal). Some of Resonant's best writing and voice performances live down here, and it snaps me back into the game.
Further in, there's a massively unexpected appearance of a whole other genre that will delight a lot of people (I was bewildered and appreciative), and I love it when the game goes hard into the special interest subjects and shows me intense pockets of drama happening in a forgotten corner of the subway. Dylan's thing is drawing, and there's an art-therapy-esque feature where he'll see something that reminds him of a memory that he can recreate with found objects and sketch; assembling these makeshift tableaus is silly and charming but I didn't take it seriously until the game wanted me to make a dragon out of rubbish and subway cones and I couldn't find the last piece. I want to finish that dragon, and it will haunt me until I do.
Remedy projects are visually and technically lovely to behold, and this one is no different. The game looks good, period. I love the FBC uniform design here, with the paper bag-like headwear that feels like a page from the Venture Bros henchman universe. I will eat up every second of Matthew Porretta's screentime as Casper Darling, and I love a good bit of stylised shadow puppetry. These are all load-bearing parts of the Control universe. But there's only so much you can do to spice up a repeated landscape of city blocks and same-y military blockades without losing aesthetic potency. Naturally there are big moments of spectacle – visual spectacle is likewise a pillar of the Control experience – but after a certain point it feels like Resonant leans a bit too much on quirky weirdness (weird dogs! floating vending machines! warring aliens!) in New York, as a stand-in for narrative quality and substance. Not much comes close to the "oh shit, cool" moments or impeccable vibes that made Control special.
I don't think anyone expects perfect coherence from an SCP-inspired setting, and honestly I don't think it matters that the game isn't entirely clear about its ending, either. But there's something missing. Perhaps it's the sense that the game tried to incorporate too much, and spread itself too wide. The contrast between Control's maximalist approach to paratextual storytelling and its minimalist design felt sharp and savvy. Resonant, though, feels like it's trying to have too many fingers in too many pies.
I realise that Remedy rebukes the idea of Control Resonant being an open-world game, and it's not quite as freewheeling and permissive as that, but Resonant feels like it's chasing the hallmarks of a live-service game while trying, only partly successfully, to echo the very deliberate structure and style of the genre storytelling that worked so well in the first game. You cannot make a good game whose whole cryptic conceit hinges on smart unconventional worldbuilding, and also shoehorn in the most deadening part of MMOs – world events, the equivalent of daily chores – without bringing the whole narrative party down. It's not a question of giving us something we haven't seen before. It's a question of being able to sustain that distinct, uncanny weirdness that brought Control to life. And to expand on that core magic, without muddying what made it special in the first place.
A copy of Control Resonant was provided for this review by Remedy Entertainment.

item.description:
Nintendo is having a pretty good time of it at the moment. Last year, we learned that the Switch 2 became the fastest selling video game hardware device in US history, usurping the PS4's golden record. Then, earlier this year, we learned that Switch 2 sales reached nearly 20m almost one year after release, making it the second-fastest selling console in US history. Buoyed by the runaway successes of games like Pokopia and other first-party hits, not even the reality of a hardware price rise seems to be hobbling Nintendo's momentum.
And it seems the company is keen to keep this pace up. "We're at the beginning of Nintendo Switch 2," says Nintendo of America COO, Devon Pritchard in an interview with Variety. "This is just beginning and we've already had some really wonderful experiences, both ours and third-party come to the table and I can't wait to see what the system is going to do and what our talented developers will bring to the table."
She goes on to point out that the publisher's success isn't just in hardware and software, but in Nintendo's recently acquired popularity at the box office, too. "We're working with Sony Pictures. We are going to have a movie come out in the end of April," she notes, referring to The Legend of Zelda. "We're very excited about that". No doubt; Nintendo and Illumination earned $1bn from The Super Mario Galaxy Movie at the last count, pulling in a third of that ($372.6m) in the opening weekend alone.
Whilst Pritchard is certainly excited about the games the company has on the docket - she namechecks The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, specifically - it seems her eyes are drawn more readily to the film partnerships. "But again, those partnerships and touchpoints with companies like Sony and Sony Pictures around how we can bring those experiences more broadly to not only our current players and fans but to new ones," she says, "I think that's one of the most exciting things for us over the next few years."
Safe to say, then, that Nintendo is putting a lot of effort into its expanding cinematic world. The last we heard about the next big project - The Legend of Zelda film which is just called "The Legend of Zelda", sans subtitle - was in a dedicated Zelda Direct at the beginning of September. We've not even seen a proper trailer yet, but we know that the initial shoot has wrapped filming in New Zealand (after starting the shoot in October 2025). So here's hoping we see some footage of the final product soon.
"There are more channels for content than ever before," Pritchard concludes when asked about how Nintendo plans to stand out in a media landscape more competitive than ever before. "Content is available 24/7. So I think you hear a lot of times, people saying, we are competing for consumers' time and I think what's unique is that Nintendo is focused instead on building experiences that create relationships that last generations. And I think that's a different kind of focus for us. But that really is where we put our time and our energy... how do we create those fun experiences? And that becomes the test: is something fun? It sounds simple, of course it's not."
Lets see if the company's belief in its product and audience lasts through the current industry woes; the combination of an industry crunch, rising hardware prices, and lower consumer spend is having a pretty disasterous effect elsewhere - but it seems Nintendo is so far weathering the storm.

item.title: Rockstar has remained very tight-lipped about GTA 6's multiplayer component, the potential successor to GTA 5's incredibly popular Grand Theft Auto Online, not yet commenting on whether it will even launch one. All we know currently is that when Grand Theft Auto 6 arrives on 19th November, it'll only include the single-player campaign. Read more
item.description:
But, in an interview with Bloomberg, Twitch CEO Dan Clancy has seemingly revealed GTA 6 multiplayer's launch window. "We spent a lot of time talking with Rockstar about their plans, and also helping them think about how they can engage our creators," he said. "You are going to see this big bump with GTA 6, but then an even bigger one next year when they launch multiplayer."
Here, it's worth noting that GTA 5's GTA Online mode arrived two weeks after the main game launched, but Red Dead Online - the multiplayer mode for Red Dead Redemption 2, and a more recent indicator of how Rockstar handles these staggered rollouts - went live seven months after launch.
The 'next year' referenced by Clancy here is, of course, wonderfully vague. It suggests we could see GTA Online Mk. II (that's a name I'm giving it, not anything official) launch as early as January, some two months after the big single-player release, or as far out as the end of 2027. What's more likely, though, is that we'll see a similar cadence to Red Dead Redemption 2, with GTA Online coming closer to summer than spring.
If you're worried about Rockstar dropping support for the current iteration of GTA Online, I wouldn't be too concerned. In 2025, Strauss Zelnick, boss of Rockstar parent company Take-Two, told IGN it's smart when it comes to legacy brands, and knows that people don't necessarily drop their old toys just because there are new ones on the shelves.
"I'm going to speak theoretically only because I'm not going to talk about a particular project when an announcement hasn't been made," Zelnick explained. "But generally speaking, we support our properties when the consumers are involved with those titles. As an example, we launched NBA 2K Online in China, I think originally in 2012 if I'm not mistaken. And then we launched NBA 2K Online 2 in China in 2017, if I'm not mistaken. We did not sunset Online 1. They both are still in the market and they serve consumers and they're alive and we have this massive audience."
"So we've shown a willingness to support legacy titles when a community wants to be engaged with them."
This latest news follows another flurry of GTA 6 announcements in the run-up to its November release. This week, we got word of the inevitable GTA 6 soundtrack, and last week saw all Grand Theft Auto 6's worldwide unlock times revealed ( Xbox owners can seemingly still use the old 'New Zealand trick' to play early, if they want to). Ahead of launch day, it's also worth remembering that multiple retailers have issued warnings that GTA 6 codes are region-locked, so make sure you're buying the right copy for the region you're in.
Amid the build-up to GTA 6's release, Rockstar Games and the Independent Workers Union of Great Britain (IWGB) are currently engaged in the final tribunal hearing relating to the sudden firing of 31 Rockstar North employees nearly a year ago, allegedly as part of a union-busting initiative by Rockstar.

Aside from the "return of Xbox" new CEO Asha Sharma promised awhen taking over, which enacted the announcement of 3,200 layoffs and four studio departures, we've also seen mass layoffs in other studios, too: Bungie, EA, PUBG Productions, Take-Two, Warner Bros., Epic, and many, many more have been impacted this year so far.

He notes how the typical process in Japan, when a studio needs to remove staff from its budget sheet, is to focus on contractors based outside of the country, rather than target local workers "to protect core staff in Japan".
"Everyone calls out Nintendo, but you can look at Konami or Capcom – these companies all have staff retention of 97 percent plus," Satvat told Edge, talking about what Western studios could learn from Japanese developers. "My understanding is that, generally, Japanese teams tend to be much smaller and leaner. They didn't get swept up in the live-service trend, or into these mega-blockbusters with 500-person teams. [And then there's] the executive salaries. They still make great money, but it's two or three million dollars, not 30 million." Notable here is the $38.6m salary awarded to EA boss Andrew Wilson last year. Take-Two's Strauss Zelnick earned $42.1m in 2022 - which has almost certainly increased since then. Both companies laid off staff this year.
It's worth noting here that via Satvat's own tracker, 57,628 jobs were lost across the whole industry in the period between 2022-2026. In 2026 alone, 96 percent of all the jobs lost in the video games industry were in North America and Europe. "There was a 12-to-18-month period where I estimated that over half of layoffs, globally, were in California," Satvat added. "I think this is as bad as the '83 crash if you're a game developer based in North America or western Europe, in a traditional triple-A studio. That is ground zero for the destruction."
Perhaps that's why we've seen Capcom continue its victory lap this year with games like Pragmata, Resident Evil Requiem, and Onimusha. Or why Nintendo is consistenly breaking sales records. Or why we're seeing Koei Tecmo explicitly state it believes in smaller titles to fuel its continued successes.

item.description:
The Valor Mortis developer has announced the game's price and offered an explanation as to why the team picked this particular price point. Valor Mortis costs $40 / €40, which is notably cheaper than other games releasing around the same time. We've asked for clarification on UK price.
The developer posted a message on X explaining its decision, saying that while it's confident in the game, it understands that players' time and money are at a premium in this period.
"We have had many discussions over the past year about the price of Valor Mortis. We believe the game has the quality, fidelity, and playtime in its 20-hour story to go toe-to-toe with many 'full price' titles," the developer wrote. "Still, this fall is stacked and there's high demand for your time and money."
Valor Mortis is the ambitious first-person Soulslike from Ghostrunner developer One More Level. It launches 13th October, notably in close proximity to Gears of War: E-Day, Ace Combat 8, Star Wars: Galactic Racer, Final Fantasy Resonance, and Phantom Blade Zero in October alone. It's also within striking distance of several big September releases such as Marvel's Wolverine, Silent Hill: Townfall, and Control Resonant - which you may recall is the game that caused Valor Mortis to be pushed back to October from its original 24th September release date.
There's a Deluxe Edition, priced $60 / €60. It includes the base game, a "major story DLC" coming in 2027, alongside a pack of weapon skins. Free updates are in the works, the developer promises, and will arrive in the weeks and months ahead.
Blake Rochkind, head of Valor Mortis publisher Lyrical Games, spoke to The Game Business about the agonising pricing decision and why it ultimately had to be made.
"My biggest concern was that it would send the wrong message about the game," Blake Rochkind told host Chris Dring. "So we wanted to make sure that we send the right message to the consumer about why this is, and hopefully help them understand that this is a decision we're making out of confidence for the game."
Rochkind pointed out Valor Mortis is one of the few games based on a new intellectual property releasing in one of the busiest release seasons in the games industry's history, potentially making it even harder for the publisher to convince players to buy it.
"The cards we've been dealt is [that] we are one of the only new IPs launching this fall," he explained. "We are pretty confident in Valor Mortis. It is a great game. I'm very, very excited for people to play it. But ultimately, I think the worst thing we could do is not push our chips in and say, 'We want this to be a game that you can pick up alongside these other great games.'"
Valor Mortis is in development for PC, PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. It is a day-one release on Game Pass on PC and Xbox.

item.title: Destiny being reborn within Marathon sounds like one of those ridiculous ideas fans come up with to keep their hope alive, but it's one of several "leaked" plans Bungie supposedly has, which recently made their way online. Bungie has now responded, shooting down what may be the most outlandish part of the leak. Read more
item.description:
Destiny being reborn within Marathon sounds like one of those ridiculous ideas fans come up with to keep their hope alive, but it's one of several "leaked" plans Bungie supposedly has, which recently made their way online. Bungie has now responded, shooting down what may be the most outlandish part of the leak.
"As someone who's worked on both Destiny and Marathon, I can confirm that the 'leak' about us merging the two IPs is fake," Bungie veteran and Marathon creative director Julia Nardin wrote on X. "They share a lot of the same Bungie DNA, but like siblings they're also their own independent entities. Please don't believe everything you read online."
According to the leak, Bungie is apparently "testing the waters" to merge Marathon and Destiny into a single franchise "with Marathon representing the beginning of mankind's Golden Age and to foreshadow more threats to be used in a future Destiny project."
The wide-ranging leak apparently originated from 4Chan, and was later collated on Reddit. Though it mainly involves Marathon, it does touch on Destiny in some key ways. Nardin didn't directly address any of the myriad other leaked details, however.
That merger seemingly isn't limited to narrative and lore, the post said "multiple" former Destiny 2 developers have been rehired to join the Marathon team. Some of what those Destiny 2 veterans are working on is implementing ideas - initially planned for the game's cancelled expansions and sequel, into Marathon.
Bungie delivered the final major Destiny 2 update in June after announcing all development on the game had ceased. The studio said Destiny 2 wouldn't get any any more expansions, and that Destiny 3 is not in development. Bungie laid off hundreds of workers later in the same month.
The leak claimed Marathon will 'borrow' ideas from Destiny, such as the first game's reputation and faction systems, as well as the addition of a social space. It also said Bungie will entice Destiny 2 players to try Marathon by offering in-game rewards to those who completed certain Triumphs in the game's final update - which is the most believable part of the leak.
Elsewhere in the post, it's revealed that Bungie is making Marathon free-to-play in December. That, apparently, was the reason behind the recent delay of Marathon's next major update, which is introducing a permanent PvE mode. On the subject, the leak said the mode - called Investigations - is "seen as a blend of Monster Hunter and Salmon Run from Splatoon".
"Drop in and hit the ground running with you and one-five friends clearing objectives around maps, exfilling to the next to get all the pieces together to fight large Destiny raid-style bosses," it went on.
There's more there about changes coming to certain Marathon features, the arrival of new Shells and the reworking of maps. Marathon has struggled to make an impact, having sold only an estimated 1.2 million copies at launch. On Steam, where the game's largest audience lies, player numbers have dropped to their lowest point since launch, peaking at under 3,000 concurrent players daily (via SteamDB).

Hideo Kojima took to the stage at Xbox's Tokyo Game Show 2026 broadcast today to give us an update on his two in-development games with Xbox, OD and Physint. Both games are now being published by Xbox, after we learned last week that Sony "stepped away" from Kojima Production's previously PlayStation-exclusive "action espionage" game Physint. Following the announcement, which saw Xbox take over publishing duties for the in-development title, a new report has claimed Sony's decision was the result of concerns over "budget, potential profitability and exclusivity".
Today is the first time we've seen Kojima open up about the news since the first statements announcing the split were published. "Today, I'd like to focus on [Kojima Productions'] partnership with Xbox and share with players around the world a glimpse of what's ahead," he noted during the presentation (below), before sharing that he spent time in Redmond, Washington earlier this year, spending time with Xbox boss, Asha Sharma. "There, we discussed the future of games and digital entertainment and shared a deep understanding of the goals we believe we should achieve together," Kojima explained.
First, he focused on OD-Knock, the mysterious horror game Kojima insists will be quite unlike anything we have seen before and that plenty of people will hate. He notes that development is progressing smoothly, despite performance capture and ADR recording having to be paused due to last year's SAG-AFTRA strike. "Produciton is proceeding on schedule," he confirms, before noting that Sophiua Lillis, Hunter Schafer and the team have "delivered intense and outstanding performances" which he cannot wait for us all to see. OD, he reiterates, is a new type of game that will "test the thresholds of fear". More information will be shared "down the line".
Next up, Physint. The big news here is a new collaboration with Pennywise actor Bill Skarsgård, who will play the lead role in the game. He will join previously confirmed actors such as Charlee Fraser, Don Lee, and Minami Hamabe. Kojima then shared new key art for the game, featuring a look at the costume and character Fraser and Skarsgård will play, apparently taken from a picture shot by Kojima himself at a recent photoshoot. The game is still many years from completion, but Kojima promises more news soon.
During Kojima Productions' 10th anniversary livestream, the infamous creator noted that Physint is "just the start", a vague statement that could potentially hint at Kojima seeing franchise potential in the series, though it isn't likely to happen any time soon.In 2025, Kojima noted the game won't be out for another "five or six" years, so if this is something Xbox is banking on, we can almost certainly expect it to be a marquee game for the as-yet-unrevealed Xbox Project Helix.

item.description:
Wardogs is already one of the year's biggest PC hits on Steam, but new data has revealed how its success compares to other mega-hits like Arc Raiders and Helldivers 2, as well as struggling titles like Marathon. This isn't that surprising, given Wardogs managed to sell over 1 million copies within hours of launch.
According to Alinea Analytics analyst Rhys Elliott, Wardogs has sold over 2.2 million copies so far. When aligning the game's Steam launch period with those of Arc Raiders (1.7 million) and Helldivers 2 (1 million), Wardogs' pace is clearly faster.
Of course, it remains to be seen whether Wardogs could keep up that momentum and match - or outperform - the two juggernauts' lifetime performance. Despite the differences in core gameplay and genre, Arc Raiders and Helldrivers 2 make for an excellent comparison point simply because they both launched at the same $40 (~£35) price.
One other recent $40 release that does not compare favourably to Wardogs is Bungie's Marathon. Elliott revealed Wardogs has now made more money than Marathon across all platforms, despite only being available on a single one. Wardogs has generated $70m (~£52.2m) in revenue, earning it the number seven spot on Steam's 2026 list of new games when ranked by revenue. PlayStation and Xbox ports of Wardogs are planned, but they won't be out until sometime in 2028.
"Wardogs hits the modern pricing sweet spot, sitting below the friction point of a $70 triple-A release while capturing that chunky volume of players priced out of premium titles," Rhys Elliott wrote on X.
Elliott's analysis also revealed Wardogs converted 11 percent of its Steam Wishlists into sales. 57 percent of all the game's Steam Wishlists were made in the last month, indicating the game had "a late, hot hype cycle" as opposed to a slow burn.

item.description:
Yesterday, Helldivers 2 and Horizon Forbidden West mysteriously disappeared from the Steam store in the UK. There was no announcement about this move, nor any indication it would happen before players began noticing that neither game was listed on the digital storefront. Users that did not own the games were left unable to purchase them, however people that already had the Sony Interactive Entertainment-published titles in their libraries were still able to boot and play the games.
"An error was encountered while processing your request: This item is currently unavailable in your region," read a message when users clicked on the greyed-out storefront listings for both games.
Initially, there was a suspicion that this was an intentional move - Sony has, after all, been making noises about moving away from publishing its titles on PC over the course of this year. However, it seems this delisting snafu is a complete accident, per a new statement from Sony itself.
"We are aware of an issue affecting the availability of select titles on Steam in the UK," Sony told VGC. "We are working with Valve to address the issue. We apologise for the inconvenience." So, it seems they'll likely be back to normal soon.
It's a fairly peculair turn of events: was Sony adjusting something in the backend that caused these games to be delisted? Is this an indicator of changes to come that may have been actioned early? It's a strange situation, but at least for now it seems the UK (and Isle of Man) are going to be able to get both Helldivers 2 and Horizon Forbidden West available on Steam again.
Given the conversation around PlayStation games on PC - with PlayStation exec Hermen Hulst, for example, confirming the company's narrative single-player games will now be exclusive to PS5 going forward - it's hard not to view this development with a little suspicion.

item.title: Brace yourselves, everyone: the Monster Hunter Wilds Ascendance marketing machine is spinning up. item.description:
Brace yourselves, everyone: the Monster Hunter Wilds Ascendance marketing machine is spinning up. Today, at Tokyo Game Show, Capcom released the an extended cut of the first official trailer for Ascendance, revealing the explosion-loving leonine monster, Teostra, as a huntable foe.
The infamously tricky Elder Dragon was first introduced way back in Monster Hunter 2 in 2006, its penchanct for blast effects and flame breath pushing the PS2 tech quite hard at the time. Though the developer has made some pretty decent improvements to how the game runs since launch, it does seem that the beast's fiery attacks chew up the bitrate in the trailer a little. Here's hoping that isn't a reflection of the performance in-game.
One thing I did notice in this trailer is that the infamously tricky Teo fight looks even harder in the footage we've seen so far. Granted, the trailer is only three minutes-long (the real fight will probably take 10x that, in real-time), but it seems Capcom has given everyone's favourite exploding lion a little more utility than we saw in his last appearance in Monster Hunter Rise - Sunbreak.
Teostra has long had a signature move that sees it divebomb you whilst setting off multi-blast novas (I love this game), but now Capcom looks to have given the beast charging follow-ups, too. That means, I think, that if you do manage to 'superman' dive out of the way of his AOE blasts, you will be faced with a massive, angry lion chasing you into walls or smacking you out of the air. Delicious. It looks like we're going to need perfect dodges and/or perfect blocks in order to come out on top there.
We're going to get some more tools to make this a bit easier, at least. The developer is introducing a 'Boost Bracer' for us to play with. "Build Boost Bracer energy by staying aggressive with your attacks, then activate Boost with a special Boost Driver attack, or other unique actions per weapon," Capcom explained previously. "Boost enables abilities such as new combos and enhanced attacks, allowing you to seize control of the powerful threats that await you." It seems this new mechanic will focus on offensive play, letting us soak up damage or counter attacks more readily than previous movesets allowed. Does this mean we'll be able to 'boost into' Teo's blasts, maybe dodging the first, negating the second, and then letting loose with a juiced-up combo to take advantage of the beast when he's recovering from his onslaught? God, I hope so.
One of the core complaints about Monster Hunter Wilds from launch was how easy it was, especially compared to previous games in the series. But, with various patches since and this new expansion, it seems Capcom has taken the feedback seriously. If you played the Final Fantasy 14 crossover that introduced Omega Planetes, you'll be familiar with this new, improved difficutly. That fight was not easy.
"Monster Hunter Wilds: Ascendance players can also look forward to several refinements to further improve their gameplay experience, including faster weapon swapping without the use of a Seikret mount, changing equipment outside the tent with the Item Box, and more," adds Capcom in the video description for the trailer. "These improvements will also be available in the Monster Hunter Wilds base game."
"Hunters can look forward to battling the fire-breathing Elder Dragon when the massive expansion launches in 2027," says Capcom in a press release. We don't have any word on when that might be, specifically, just yet, however. If you're keen for more Monster Hunting goodness, though, you will at least be able to play the game on Switch 2 when it launches on 4th December.

item.title: A new PlayStation 5 firmware update has officially arrived for everyone, after about a month of testing. The change log for firmware version 26.06-14.00.00 has changed in one major way since the beta first went live in August. Read more
item.description:
A new PlayStation 5 firmware update has officially arrived for everyone, after about a month of testing. The change log for firmware version 26.06-14.00.00 has changed in one major way since the beta first went live in August.
The Community Activity widget is now available for all players to add to their console's Welcome Hub. Community Activity wasn't part of the firmware's beta, but Sony has been testing the feature since May.
Community Activity has two views: Trending Now, and Top 10. Trending Now shows a list of 10 multiplayer games (or multiplayer modes within games) that are rising in popularity across PlayStation. This is where you can expect to see recently-updated games, hot new releases and games that got a sale bump. Each game tile also shows what pushed the game to get on that list, such as a surge in matches or hours played.
Top 10 is more straightforward, and it shows a list of the 10 most popular games over the last week. This ranking varies depending on your country or region, making it more accurate. You can probably expect these to be roughly the same week-to-week, though, if previous data is anything to go by. The only problem? Top 10 used to list player counts for each game in the beta, but that is gone from the final version.
You can see the difference between the beta from May (via TechPowerUp) and the current version (via SpawnPoint). The change is notable as it signaled at the time Sony may be following Steam's lead in showing player counts for games on its platform, even if the feature was never as granular or real-time.
Two other major features of firmware 26.06-14.00.00 have made it out unchanged from the beta. Those being the toggle to enable PlayStation's image upscaling tech (PSSR) by default on PS5 Pro, and the option to turn off Bluetooth at the console level in certain regions.

item.title: Joe Brammer, CEO of Bulkhead, the developer behind The Turing Test, Battalion 1944, and now the hugely successful new release Wardogs, has found himself in somewhat hot water, following a revealing interview where he discussed work culture at the UK studio. Read more
item.description:
Joe Brammer, CEO of Bulkhead, the developer behind The Turing Test, Battalion 1944, and now the hugely successful new release Wardogs, has found himself in somewhat hot water, following a revealing interview where he discussed work culture at the UK studio.
After a day of heated social media debate and an initial response via X, Brammer has now issued a statement to Eurogamer. In it, he explains the exact nature of the studio's "crunch" practices, and clarifies that his mention of monitoring the social media of potential applicants to the studio - a potential legal grey area in the UK - was a case of "speaking informally about our culture".
"A lot of people who may have an issue with crunch - rightly so, I understand that issue, we always try and avoid it, but we don't hide that this is going to happen at some point," he told podcast host Chris Dring. "[Those people] often don't make it in the door, because we want to be known for that: this is a place you come to work hard. If you care about the work you're making and the result of what you make here, this is a place to work. You'll feel really valued. If you don't, you will feel slave-driven," Brammer explained. "It's a constant to-and-fro with that."
"But we will check people's socials, and if you're constantly tweeting anti-crunch messaging: 'This should never ever be a thing', we know that and go, 'Look, you're not going to be happy here, so we're not going to go with you'."
"No information says mandatory, they made this up," said Brammer, before going on to list a number of other "facts" - some of which were discussed in the interview, such as having a four-day work week for half of the game's development time, 80 percent of shares being owned by 50 percent of staff, "everyone" at the studio being given the month of December off work, and that the studio "made a game you like and our staff will be rewarded for it accordingly".
"We made that choice, don't take it out of context, watch the whole interview here to make up your own mind," he added on X.
While Brammer may not have explicitly said crunch at Bulkead was "mandatory", earlier in his interview with The Game Business he did state that it's a known expectation of his. When asked about his forthright approach to public communication, he said: "At Bulkhead and online, people know what I believe. They know I don't believe in work from home for making video games. They know I don't stand for that. They know I expect people to crunch. I own that. I don't try and hide it."
"That doesn't mean that we also didn't try and do the four-day work week and make workplaces better. They know I care about my team and my very close team," he went on.
Crunch is an especially thorny topic amongst those who work in video games today, with the industry having a long history of normalising the practice of enforced, or otherwise heavily implied, overtime. Years of reporting has revealed a trend of labour exploitation at several high-profile studios, from CD Projekt Red to Rockstar Games, and a culture of mandating crunch ahead of major milestones at studios such as Naughty Dog. While in many cases crunch is not explicitly mandated, reporting has consistently evidenced that personal passion or other forms of internal pressure can be weaponised to get people to work longer hours. Many studios, including those reported on above, have gone on to promise to eradicate the practice going forward.
On the podcast, when asked what crunch actually looks like at the studio, Brammer said it depends on the context. "Generally, it depends on what age you are, is what we're seeing," he said. "The older guys are like, 'This isn't crunch, this is mild overtime,'" he answered. "But to do that, we have to be very conscious and supportive of our own staff and try and coach them to know when it's enough, when it's not enough."
"In terms of defining what it is," he added, "I always use the analogy of life being a balancing act. And sometimes, if you ask someone to mimic balancing, they put two hands out kind of like they're on a tightrope," he said, holding his hands out evenly either side of him. "But really, it's probably more like this," he continued, tipping his hands up and down on either side.
"And for the last three months, Wardogs has been a lot more important than a lot of their family lives. It has been, because that's what pays the money for them. But now, Bulkhead and me have to acknowledge that it needs to go the other way. So for example, everyone's pushing us to get console [versions] out earlier and we've just said: No, you don't understand, that's not how it's gonna work. You can't - we can't push [the development team] more. We're not doing that. It's going to release in 2028 when we say it's going to release.
"So for me it's about balance, and helping people and making sure that they have a company where they can say, 'I'm tapping out' and not feel like they're going to get fired for tapping out."
Meanwhile, when asked how that culture of sporadic crunch remains feasible with an industry that's getting older and less able to move their life around work, Brammer said the studio has tried a few things to mixed success. "So for instance, we once tried to do paternity leave and give people 10 weeks paternity and it was a disaster. Because they took the 10 weeks - as they should - but their partners, when it got to week 11, could not handle them leaving. They couldn't handle the fact that they're on their own with a kid now. And it was super consistent," he explained.
"So we went the other way: two weeks paternity, the bare minimum. And then what we said was, the third week you come back half day, just the morning. I don't care if you do no work, you're training your partner how to look after their first child together and you're building a routine. And then the third week, you do full days for two of the days or whatever. And then what we say is we're going to give you three weeks to use as paternity weeks across the entire year for the first year. Because as you know, the first two weeks are actually kind of easy for a lot of people… it gets a lot harder later."
Responding to the above discussion, Brammer issued the following statement on the topic of crunch to Eurogamer:
"In June 2026 we were late for the Wardogs beta build. In this instance I apologised and said the only way I thought we could get the game into beta, was by working an extra 2 hours a day Monday through Thursday, for 4 weeks (16 working days total). We admitted to the staff that this was crunch; we clearly stated that we needed to crunch. It was optional; four people opted out, nothing happened to them and nothing will. But I can admit that maybe the social pressure within a very tight-knit team might make those individuals feel less than great.
"The reason it was 2 hours and not something else was build times. Extending slightly meant we could get x1 more build per day, review it and get QA's pass back on it, instead of waiting on the nightly build and picking it up the following morning.
"In this interview, I spoke a lot about trying to do things differently at Bulkhead. We don't always follow "how things should be done" because we haven't always had that experience, and the credit for giving us the freedom to experiment goes entirely to our staff.
"The best-known example is our four-day working week, which we ran for two years and, at the time, was one of the largest trials of its kind. We ultimately needed the fifth day of productivity, but we saw huge benefits and absolutely aspire to bring some form of it back in the future.
"Something mentioned far less is that 80 percent of Bulkhead's shares are owned by 50 percent of our staff. The founders chose to give up equity to make that happen, and it's one of the things I'm proudest of here."
Eurogamer put this to Bulkhead, in response to which Brammer provided the following statement:
"We understand your concern, but I was speaking informally about our culture and the kind of environment we have at Bulkhead, rather than setting out our formal recruitment process.
"Where we do consider publicly available information as part of recruitment, it is done in line with applicable UK employment and data protection law. We don't access private accounts or carry out covert or intrusive checks.
Elsewhere in the interview, Brammer discussed several other topics revolving around the notion of Bulkhead "doing things differently", including why the studio avoids featuring trailers in Geoff Keighley's showcases such as The Game Awards, the studio's intentionally open approach to communication - including his invitation to disgruntled beta players to apply for a refund and come back when the studio had improved things, accompanied by a tongue-in-cheek trailer titled "10 reasons NOT to buy" - and Brammer's occasional frustrations with UK labour laws.
In this case, that frustration was in reference to his attempts to reduce working hours or provide better work-life balance. "What's quite frustrating is I find British HR laws quite restrictive to wanting to do better things," he said. "The four-day work week, for example, was very restrictive. We had to get around laws to make the four-day work week possible. And I think when we try and do something a bit different, again, we hit blockages."
It was a similar issue in regards to Bulkhead's above approach to paternity leave. "That again - do you know what, I'll be honest - you can interpret that in HR law as [some] people being given more holiday than others who are not in the same position," he said. "So you can actually go, 'That's not fair!' but we're just like, 'sue us', at this point, this is ridiculous."
Wardogs itself has been incredibly successful, selling 2 million copies in its first five days of release on Steam. Brammer revealed in the same interview that some members of the team - such those who own shares in the company - will receive bonuses as a result of that success.
"If we're going to be a company who says, 'We do crunch', then we have to also say, 'But you get something for it.' We want people to know that those people who do work hard get that return, and it is life-changing," Brammer concluded in the interview.
"I'm going to be really excited to see juniors who have been with us for two or three years who are going to get money to buy a house, or at least a down payment."

item.title: Another round of layoffs is seemingly sweeping through Build A Rocket Boy, the studio responsible for MindsEye and founded by GTA veteran Leslie Benzies. The studio's future is now uncertain. Read more
item.description:
Another round of layoffs is seemingly sweeping through Build A Rocket Boy, the studio responsible for MindsEye and founded by GTA veteran Leslie Benzies. The studio's future is now uncertain.
Reported on by IGN, more staff working at Build A Rocket Boy have said they've been let go. Head of audio Stuart Ross, level designer Liam Shannon, release manager Michaela Emslie, lead QA analyst Sandy Greig, QA analyst Elizabet Tyaneva, production QA analyst Cameron Deaves, and many more recently announced their time at the studio is coming to a close.
This certainly isn't the first time Build A Rocket Boy has cut jobs following the messy launch (and even more messy aftermath) of MindsEye. Last year, the company made an unknown number of staff redundant. In May, the studio reportedly laid off a further 170 workers. Remaining staff also staged a protest this summer against Build A Rocket Boy's "all expenses paid" fan event.
These most recent layoffs also call into question the future of the entire company. Kotaku reports that sources close to the studio claim Build A Rocket Boy is permanently shutting down.
Adding fuel to the fire, in a recent LinkedIn post, principal talent acquisition officer Dan Hawkins said he's looking for new work "along with the rest of my colleagues at Build A Rocket Boy," and he's now "seeing BARB through till the very end, helping wrap things up here in the HR department."
MindsEye itself hasn't been able to turn around a turbulent first year. The game was initially promised to be part of Everything, a make-your-own-game type of Roblox-y experience, before the scale was pulled back considerably.
Eurogamer's one-star review said MindsEye was "sunk by a ridiculous story, inconsistent writing, poorly designed mission scenarios, and utterly atrocious combat." A myriad of tech issues certainly didn't help its case. From there, executives from the studio held firm that MindsEye suffered at the hands of unnamed saboteurs.

item.title: Arguably Monster Hunter Wilds' most egregious microtransaction is being retired, and, soon, you'll be able to edit your hunters and cat-friend Palicos whenever you like, as many times as you like. Read more
item.description:
Arguably Monster Hunter Wilds' most egregious microtransaction is being retired, and, soon, you'll be able to edit your hunters and cat-friend Palicos whenever you like, as many times as you like.
Publisher Capcom waved goodbye to the divisive Edit Vouchers earlier today. Starting from 3 December, the vouchers will be pulled from all digital storefronts and players will instead get 10 Character Edit Vouchers and 10 Palico Edit Vouchers for free.
Those vouchers should tide you over until the release of Monster Hunter Wilds: Ascendance sometime next year, at which point "all players will be able to re-edit the appearance of their hunter and Palico as many times as they like, free of charge and without the need for a Character Edit Voucher." Even if you're not planning on picking up the Ascendance expansion, you'll still be able to give your characters a makeover ad nauseum, I should add.
Mildly whelming news for anyone who's already spent real-world money on rejigging your big beast battlers: you won't be refunded, but Capcom will give you an in-game pendant set "as a token of our appreciation." You can claim the Special Thank-You Pendant Set, which includes the Heavenly Hog and Beelzeboar pendants, starting from 3 December, as well. Gosh, this series has the best monster names.
"The pendants listed above may become available separately at a later date," Capcom wrote in its announcement.
While Monster Hunter Wilds came out the gate swinging, its stamina has taken quite a big hit in the year since - thanks largely to the game's questionable PC performance.
The game regularly gets outsold by its older siblings, though Capcom is taking measures to close the gap between Wilds and World, to its credit. The publisher recently hoped a price drop, a generous demo and next year's expansion could help Wilds catch up to the monstrous hits that came before it. Monster Hunter Wilds' Switch 2 port should also help matters come December, alongside the welcome quality-of-life updates we've been receiving as of late.

item.title: Nighthawks just got a happy ending. Developers of the vampiric RPG have successfully removed the game's 'Adult Only' rating on Steam - a label that would have otherwise hidden the game from most players. Read more
item.description:
Nighthawks just got a happy ending. Developers of the vampiric RPG have successfully removed the game's 'Adult Only' rating on Steam - a label that would have otherwise hidden the game from most players.
The latest victim of Valve's vague updated guidelines, Nighthawks was accidentally slapped with an 'Adult Only' rating mere days before the text-based role-playing game was due to come out on the platform. The tag would've exiled Nighthawks to the shadow realm, stopping it from appearing in Steam searches and removing it from view entirely in certain countries. Thankfully, Nighthawks escaped just in time for its launch on 22 September. (Good spot, RPS.)
"Last weekend, Nighthawks was mistakenly classified as 'Adults Only' by Valve. This put Nighthawks into a category usually reserved for porn games and rendered it almost invisible on the Steam storefront," the developers write in a statement posted to Steam. "At the risk of disappointing some players, Nighthawks is not porn. Sexy? Sure. Deals with mature themes? Definitely. Porn? Most definitely not. Anyone playing Nighthawks expecting lots of sex and nudity will leave very disappointed. Any sexy scenes are text only, and the few scenes with nudity are presented with strategically placed props and hands covering up the naughty bits."
While the debacle kept the team scrambling for a few days, they acknowledged that Valve were apparently "very helpful in expediting the review on our appeal so we could get the AO rating dropped." The devs still aren't sure exactly what made Valve's flaming red eye turn on them, either, but the scandal supposedly doubled the game's wishlists.
"Well, it was stressful to go through and we were basically swimming in cortisol the past few days, but I'd be lying if I said it wasn't a net positive," the statement continued. "When I posted my frustrations on social media, I did not expect it to go viral. We got some press coverage out of it and wishlists essentially doubled overnight. All good things! I wish I could say I planned this as a guerrilla marketing stunt, but I'm not that dumb and I’m not that smart!
I am also very aware that I am extremely lucky to have the fanbase and the (relative) clout to make a bit of noise and get this handled quickly. Many devs in the same situation wouldn’t be able to do that. At the very least, our situation has made Valve aware that this is a problem many indies making mature games may face during the submission process. Hopefully it means that others will have an easier time of it going forward."
The Nighthawks devs aren't the only folks who have been struggling with Steam and Itch.io's increased stringency. Multiple queer developers spoke out against both storefront's restrictive content guidelines last year. Robert Yang also tried to battle censorship with a compilation of his award-winning games. And satirical open-world Future? No Thanks was very recently subject to a very similar situation because of the game's mild nudity, as well.

item.title: The Blood of Dawnwalker director Konrad Tomaszkiewicz has told me the game's divisive time mechanic - which gives you a limited amount of time to save your family, and attaches a time-cost to every quest and notable action you do in the game - won't necessarily feature in a sequel. item.description:
The Blood of Dawnwalker director Konrad Tomaszkiewicz has told me the game's divisive time mechanic - which gives you a limited amount of time to save your family, and attaches a time-cost to every quest and notable action you do in the game - won't necessarily feature in a sequel.
In an interview this afternoon, I asked Tomaszkiewicz whether the time mechanic was central to Dawnwalker's identity, as a series. Developer Rebel Wolves has talked openly about wanting to make more games, but Tomaszkiewicz is unsure if the time mechanic will return.
"We didn't decide it, to be honest," Tomaszkiewicz said. "We will play with it. If we will have parts of the story, or the whole story, to which it fits, then we will use it. If we will have stories where it does not fit, we will not force it. We will play with this system and we will try to use it to boost the urgency of some events in the game. But I'm not saying that in every game we will have the same scheme or loop - it's not like this.
"We are also considering and researching some other crazy ideas which can make the RPG genre different to surprise people in the future," he added.
The time mechanic in The Blood of Dawnwalker gives you 30 days and 30 nights to rescue your family from the clutches of the vampire antagonist in the game, Brencis. A time gauge, broken into segments, advances when you complete quests or move to their next stage, but also when you spend points in some skills. But time doesn't just dribble away when exploring the world and tussling with miscellaneous enemies like wolves - you have to more deliberately move time on.
Nevertheless, it's a mechanic that's proved divisive ever since it was first announced, with many RPG players saying they don't want to feel hurried in a game, or that they don't want to have to play a game more than once to see everything it has to offer - the completionist mindset. The most popular mod, pre-launch, took the mechanic out entirely.
"There are a lot of complaints about the time mechanics," Tomaszkiewicz acknowledged, "and there are two groups of people fighting with each other and so on. This is our [unique selling point], and I know that there are the mods [that remove the time mechanic]. If someone wants to play on the mod, it's fine, but I want to encourage people to try this implementation we have, because first of all we balanced it in a way that it's possible to do around 80 percent of the content with the time mechanic so it's not so bad.
"The arguments of 'I want to see everything in one playthrough' I understand, but it's false to begin with, because even in games like The Witcher, you cannot see everything in one playthrough because you have choices and consequences, and different things happen when you choose different things [excluding other outcomes]. The time mechanic somehow adds to that, but if it's so much, I don't think so." So even if you turn the time mechanic off, you won't necessarily see everything.
But Tomaszkiewicz reiterated that he understands people have "really strong feelings" about it. "I'm getting these messages even privately," he said, smiling. "I knew that it would be a problem. But what is funny is that in the beginning, after the release of the game, there were a lot of those voices, but right now it's a lot less because a lot of people finish the game already.
"They think that they have more time than they need, actually," he added, "and they can do more than they thought they could. And I believe that as more and more people finish the game, these proportions will be different. There will always be people who will have a problem with that because they don't like time mechanics at all, but I think that is fine. They can download the mod or and you know and play without it if they want."
I reviewed The Blood of Dawnwalker for Eurogamer and came away liking the time mechanic, believing it added a time-presence so many other RPGs lack, though I had some issues with it as well. I put these issues to Tomaszkiewicz in our interview - and many more besides - to Tomaszkiewicz in our fuller interview, which I'll publish on Eurogamer early next week.

item.title: Fable developer Playground Games has said "many people within Xbox view Fable as being vital to the DNA of the platform", which is why this game has been allowed such a long and "protected" development. Read more
item.description:
Fable developer Playground Games has said "many people within Xbox view Fable as being vital to the DNA of the platform", which is why this game has been allowed such a long and "protected" development.
Ralph Fulton, director of the Fable reboot, revealed these details in an interview with The Guardian. "I genuinely think Fable is an important game," Fulton said. "What has protected us over a long development cycle is that so many people within Xbox view Fable as vital to the DNA of the platform. I would go a step further and say it's important to video games as a whole. It offers a combination of elements that simply doesn't exist anywhere else."
The Fable reboot was announced in 2020, though its existence had been talked about years earlier, and it marked a surprising change for Playground Games which had until then been known for racing games like Forza Horizon.
Actual development on Fable reportedly started in 2016, and the game has seemingly weathered multiple shake-ups, including the departure of the game's narrative lead in 2023. With Fable now set for release in 2027, it will be nearly seven years since it was officially announced.
Elsewhere in the interview, Fulton referenced the impressive line-up of comedic British talent in the game, including It Crowd's Richard Ayoade and What We Do in the Shadows' Natasia Demetriou. "Richard Ayoade virtually improvised a new script for his scenes on the spot," Fulton said. "Listening to him conjure that dialogue was one of my favourite days on this project. Natasia Demetriou brought a level of British swearing to her character that honestly shocked us, but it's brilliant and we let her run with it.”
Fulton also emphasised the importance of delivering a satisfying finale, even though prevalent statistics show relatively few players see games through to their end. "It's easy to look at industry metrics saying 100 percent of people start a game and only 25 percent finish, and decide not to invest heavily in the finale," Fulton said. "But we relentlessly pursued quality here.
"In great Fable fashion, it culminates in a choice that really challenges you to think about who you are, with a real personal cost to weigh against the outcome."
Fable arrives 23rd February on PC, PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. It's the first Fable game to launch on PlayStation.

item.title: HBO boss Casey Bloys has mentioned again that he believes The Last of Us series will be finished in three seasons. Read more
item.description:
HBO boss Casey Bloys has mentioned again that he believes The Last of Us series will be finished in three seasons.
Speaking to Deadline at an Emmys afterparty, Bloys said "I think [showrunner] Craig [Mazin] has planned it as the final season," when asked if Season 3 will be the last one. Bloys said a similar thing in February, telling Deadline "it certainly seems that way", when asked whether the third season will be The Last of Us' finale.
The Last of Us Season 3 airs at some point next year, and is due to focus more on Abby's story from The Last of Us Part 2. The series separated Abby and Ellie's stories in a way that was different to the alternating structure of the games. This was one of the reasons there was a more divided reaction to the second series, after the first series had been almost universally applauded. Could this dip in audience response have influenced HBO's enthusiasm for making a fourth season?
Of course, Maizin is also hard at work adapting the beloved Baldur's Gate 3 for HBO, the project having been announced early this year. He himself is a big fan of the game, and while the game's developer Larian is not involved, it has welcomed Maizin to its offices and apparently discussed ideas with him.
