item.description:
I cannot remember the last time I put this many hours into a game for a review. And still, I'm sitting here, writing this, itching to play more of Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave. Despite some odd decisions for an RPG of this depth and scale - a single save slot and diluted difficulty, to name two - I haven't played a game that has captivated and fascinated me like this in years. This is Fire Emblem at its peak, a game as sharp and satisfying as Awakening on the 3DS, with character work and story as compelling as Three Houses. It summons the same sense of wonder and scale as those multi-disc PS1 RPGs did back in the 90s. Developer Intelligent Systems has refined all the map-building, scenario-setting work it did with Engage and iterated it alongside the storytelling tour de force of Three Houses to create something exceptional, no matter what direction you look at it from. This, right here, is a reason to buy a Switch 2.
Let's start at the end of the world, shall we? An introductory section of the game shows you the end of everything. It's up to you, mysterious God-like avatar, to rewind time to the Heroic Games of 1449 and peer into the political intrigue of the Dagdan continent to unravel how we got to this undead-filled apocalypse. It's all very anime, very high stakes and high drama, and honestly, this introductory crawl is the worst bit of the game. But, if you can stick with the megaton exposition dump and endure the slow-paced tutorial battles, you'll crack open the oddly sci-fi-flavoured carapace to feast on the rich nectar of fantasy role-playing within.
With the narrative wrapper discarded, you get to see what the game is really about: four distinct paths, following four distinct characters. You're limited to one save slot, because all the paths are intrinsically linked: you can hop between stories at will (though I'd recommend at least giving yourself some guardrails to ensure progression, otherwise you'll never make it out of Chapter 1). By 80 hours and counting, for what it's worth, I had played each of the four paths - though two were somewhat rushed for timing's sake and I played only story-critical missions for those. I reckon a full, leisurely playthrough of this game will take a good 200 hours, if you're a completionist. But even that may be conservative.
You've probably seen our core cast in the trailers: the four main protagonists are Theodora (the loyal, citizen-first warrior queen), Dietrech (a violent and intelligent foreigner determined to uncover Dagda's mysteries), Cai (a young village boy caught up in a peculiar conspiracy), and Leda (a traveling performer lusting for revenge). The quality, depth, and voice acting work across all four stories is great, though I have to single out Leda's path as the most emotive and well-acted of the lot. You've got more production value in just one of these paths than most smaller RPGs get in their entire runtime, honestly. You just have to accept that the majority of plot-first cutscenes are going to happen in one of the same 30-or-so backdrops, with very minimal over-the-shoulder camerawork. It's not really a problem though, because the writing is generally good enough to hold your attention, and the little animated portraits do more than enough to convey what's going on.
As you pluck away at the knotted, labyrinthine plot, you start to become aware of the impossibly complex web Intelligent Systems has spun here. I kept expecting to run into the same fights on the same maps in different paths, but Intelligent Systems has somehow placed and paced everything so that every single path feels different. Even when you do team up Theodora and Cai, for example, the convoluted route to get there is so different - and the final battle so twisted - that you wouldn't even really know they were the same fight without the prompts. There's probably twice as much going on here as Three Houses, and that's an ungenerous take.
It's better, too: whilst Three Houses excelled in some ways, there was a little bloat either side of the (in)famous timeskip that hampered the overall game a little - the school sections sometimes felt prolonged, and the pacing sometimes a little clumsy. Fortune's Weave has been engineered to cater more to your tastes; if you don't like the 'social simulation' side of nu-Fire Emblem, you don't have to engage with it. If you're more interested in giving the right gifts to the right people, and filling your army with just about every bonus unit imaginable, you'll need to create a spreadsheet to min-max it properly. But Intelligent Systems doesn't need you to play either way: There's more agency - and urgency, at times - in Fortune's Weave than Three Houses ever managed. I think there's a three-way split here: the opening hours of the game appeal to nu-spec Fire Emblem fans with its Persona-flavoured social focus, and Chapter 2 is more akin to the itinerant fights of 2005's Radiant Dawn or 2008's Shadow Dragon. The last portion stands alone. I won't divulge too much of that here for both spoiler and embargo reasons.
Because of the pacing - the pendulum swing between story-critical fights and languorous open world exploration - Fortune's Weave also never suffers from the weight and complexity of the plot. As you enter Chapter 2, things get a lot more streamlined: you basically need to get your army set up, your social links bolstered, your army equipped with decent weaponry and so on before you hit that first point of no return. The 'War' section of the game (sandwiched in-between the four paths of the first section and the end-game run) is an inclement gauntlet of battles, the Fire Emblem equivalent of a boss rush - where you get to see the mechanical gears that animate the great structure that Fortune's Weave is moving nakedly. Combat puzzles are artisanal and engineered with deft strategy in mind, the maps designed with variation and gimmickry, the pacing somehow both high-adrenaline and fascinating. It is, blow-by-blow, a visceral counter to the almost indolent pace of the first third of the game. The contrast is a drug, here - so potent and impactful that even on your fourth explosive entry into Chapter 2 you've barely built up any tolerance to it.
The combat, incidentally, is better than Fire Emblem has ever been. The once-simple 'rock-paper-scissors' weapon triangle is largely mooted. That simplicity has been modified by so many different weapon variations, special moves tied to different weapon types, and some interesting wrangling of classes, that it's no longer a simple case of 'mage needs to kill an armoured unit'. Don't get me wrong, I wouldn't send my pegasus-mounted swordswoman into a gaggle of archers, but each class and each unit has more utility than simply 'A beats B' this time around. To offset the more diluted specialty pool each unit has, there's more variation to victory conditions across maps than any other Fire Emblem game I've played before: there's a lot of 'kill the enemy commander', sure, but there are also gimmicks baked into the biggest fights that will make you think more about mobility, strategy, and stalling (!) than simply 'who can dish out the biggest damage'. Adding Blaze Arts for the main characters also gives very powerful abilities that cost HP, rather than weapon durability, making room for even more utility-per-character, as long as you have a decent White Mage to hand.
In some battles, the mathematical catnip of figuring out how to overwhelm enemy forces will have you grinning wildly as you mow down defenseless units with sadistic ease. Others knock onto your back foot so often, it feels like you'll never gain momentum. So when you do - when you orchestrate a flanking maneuver and break a tight formation with your splinter units that have fought tooth and nail to peel back your enemy's iron-clad defenses - you feel like a genius.
And that's where the role-playing conceit meets the strategy in Fortune's Weave. Each path's leader has a couple of 'core' army members that have special quirks or abilities that make them particularly effective fighters, usually complementing the main character very well. Having an offensive mage that can also heal on Leda's team, for example, synergises very well with how her Dance command allows allies to have a second go. The downside of this is that I found myself relying on my 'story allies' so much that I felt unmotivated to go out of my way to recruit other units in most paths. Each army does have a clear blindspot you'll need to cover if you want to overcome some of the trickier fights, though. And thanks to the writing, you'll almost certainly gravitate towards units you're going to want with you at all times (Lilian, you're the GOAT). But then, I prefer the role-playing and tight-knit realisation of my armies to expansive, impersonal ones. I get more support conversations between my core cast this way, too.
The only thing I can anticipate both newcomers and dyed-in-the-wool Fire Emblem veterans complaining about is the difficulty. This is, on regular difficulty, the easiest Fire Emblem yet - in playing through four paths, there was only one instance of permadeath I encountered. And you can rewind time for free on Normal mode. For balance, I started a new save on Hard mode and here things got a little bit spicier, with more friction that had me really going down to the wire and relying on critical hit percentages to come out of some important story battles unscathed. It's also worth noting that the pathing works for difficulty, too: if you start with Cai, you're going to get an easier story that introduces you to gentle concepts and primes you on the narrative a bit more. Go for Dietrich, and you'll be facing down more intense fights that require more strategy. Given that you can also choose either 'Classic' or 'Casual' (read: permadeath on or off), there is a lot you can do to make the game a bit more challenging, but my overall impression of Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave is that it's an easy game - especially by classic Fire Emblem standards. We can probably expect a 'Lunatic' or 'Maddening' mode in an update somewhere down the line, at least.
If you're after more of a challenge, you can take on the expansive side activities on offer between the main bouts of the Heroic Games tournament (and beyond). Each path has specific side missions to engage with - sending supplies back to your countrymen as Theodora, dancing in taverns across the land as Leda, and so on - that add a bit of variety to what is an otherwise pretty similar filler experience between the paths. The bonus battles are usually pretty easy, though, and there's this very interesting parabolic effect on difficulty as you progress. Basically, as you play, the meta-narrative revolving around your God-avatar from the start of the game comes into play.
You get rewarded 'karma crystals' for feats performed across the whole save file: play for 50 hours? Get some crystals. Kill 200 undead units? Crystals. Watch five A-level 'support conversations' because you've become besties with your whole crew? Lots of crystals. These can be used to unlock various Boons of Salvation - doubling XP earned for certain classes, getting discounts on weapons, making levelling up weapon proficiencies easier - that makes latter paths an absolute breeze. You don't have to engage with these boons, of course, but as someone playing a game like this on a deadline, I absolutely did - and it turned what could have been a soulless grind through the later paths into a fun, breezy victory tour that showed a side of Fire Emblem I've never seen before. As someone that likes to have my games punish me, doing my last path with an overpowered crew harvesting rewards their forebears manage to acquire beforehand felt really good. It showed me how fun Intelligent Systems' designs are, even when you're breaking the game a little bit. Your mileage may vary, but I'd rather have too many tools than too few when it comes to customising my experience of the game.
Ultimately, Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave represents the pinnacle of Intelligent Systems' achievements. It plaits a tapestry from all of the series' various highest highs, somehow managing to entwine the storytelling prowess of Three Houses with the clean, satisfying combat of Engage, threading a bonus party-based battle system from the 3DS title Fire Emblem Echoes: Shadows of Valentia into a world map that's bigger and better than anything we've seen in the series to date. It reminds me of Path of Radiance, at times, with its taste for drama and consequence. It is an absolute visual treat, and its lush Mediterranean setting inspired by medieval Spain makes the whole thing feel exciting and unfamiliar. Even complaints about the difficulty can be distilled into something playful - a look into how Intelligent Systems likes playing with its food, a flirtation with power fantasy and a break from the grindstone in a game all about contrasts. Fortune's Weave has an obsession with scale; but it never loses sight of the minutiae because of it - this is a game with heart, and brain. A shining jewel in the strategy RPG genre, and an essential one for the Switch 2. I can't wait to play another 80 hours.
A copy of Fire Emblem: Fortune's Weave was provided for this review by Nintendo.

item.title: The second wave of games coming to Xbox Game Pass in September has been announced, and the list considerably improves what's already on offer, with a huge new arrival in Gears of War: E-Day, and notable arrivals in Dune Awakening, and Minecraft Dungeons 2. Read more
item.description:
The second wave of games coming to Xbox Game Pass in September has been announced, and the list considerably improves what's already on offer, with a huge new arrival in Gears of War: E-Day, and notable arrivals in Dune Awakening, and Minecraft Dungeons 2.
Gears of War: E-Day needs little introduction because it's the big new Gears of War game - a prologue of sorts to the original Gears of War story, which follows Marcus Fenix and pals as they respond to the Locust invasion that later becomes known as Emergence Day, or E-Day for short. This is an important exclusive for Xbox, but will it be the banger it needs?
Dune Awakening's console debut has added interest because it brings a single-player mode to what was originally a multiplayer-first survival MMO on PC, when it launched there last summer. It's a game that's been shaking its massively multiplayer foundations since its release, in order to, presumably, appeal to more people, and with a third Dune movie arriving in December, it's a good time for it.
Minecraft Dungeons 2 we know less about. A sequel was something of a surprise when it was announced earlier in the year, and the question is how much it can build on the Diablo-like foundations of the original to fulfil the promise that Minecraft Dungeons 1 didn't - or at least not quite.
Those are the big games, but there are also some notable additions to Game Pass Premium in co-op brawler Marvel Cosmic Invasion, Planet of Lana 2, Ninja Gaiden 4, and Keeper. There are some decent games there.
Notable departures on 30th September are martial arts aging roguelike Sifu, Rebellion's Fallout-adjacent Atomfall, and creepy co-op horror Little Nightmares 2.

item.description:
Xbox could be planning another major shake-up of its Game Pass subscription service, this time removing key benefits the service is known for. That's according to a new leak from ResetEra user Slayven, who in 2025 revealed Microsoft's plans to raise Game Pass prices and change tier offerings, some of which turned out to be true.
Slayven's latest post said another rearranging of Game Pass tiers, and their names, is in the works. The service is reportedly going to drop slightly in price with the caveat of removing day-one games - new games offered on Game Pass the day they launch.
An ad-supported tier is also said to be coming, and cloud streaming is apparently being removed from Game Pass entirely. The change is reportedly due to take place between February and April 2027.
Microsoft hasn't directly addressed the specifics of the rumour but told Forbes reporter Paul Tassi that no changes are currently planned.
"We regularly test different Game Pass offerings and look at what works best for players in different markets. We don't have any changes to announce today or plans that have been finalised. There are no changes to previously announced games coming to Game Pass Ultimate on day one," Microsoft's statement read.
Beyond the volume of changes being proposed, it's unclear whether online multiplayer is included in either of the main tiers. The fate of PC Game Pass also remains unclear; Slayven said before, in 2025, it would be going away, which didn't turn out to be true.
Microsoft cut the price of Game Pass Ultimate and PC Game Pass in April, but took away Call of Duty as a day-one release while doing so. It's not unreasonable to assume another change is being planned, especially given Microsoft's recent decision to severely limit Xbox cloud streaming across all three existing Game Pass tiers; the new game time-caps are not arbitrary, reportedly set at Microsoft's break-even point.
Xbox's new CEO Asha Sharma previously said she's interested in offering new ways for players to obtain Xbox hardware and access its services. On Game Pass specifically, Sharma said in April, "we will evolve Game Pass into a more flexible system which will take time to test and learn around."

item.description:
Overnight, in the run up to Tokyo Game Show, Koei Tecmo and Team Ninja announced that Wo Long 2: Wings of Ember, the latest instalment in the studios' dark Three Kingdoms-inspired action-RPG series, will be released worldwide on 4th March 2027. The two companies also announced a huge alpha test for the game in the form of a free demo that provides an early look at the game, including an in-progress character creation system, and online multiplayer for up to three players.
The demo contains the "open field of Changban", effecitvely one entire level from the game, where you can "join forces with Liu Bei's army in fierce battles against the pursuing forces of Cao Cao, and encounter demons inspired by legendary Chinese classics." If you finish the demo, you'll get a Fledgling Phoenix Helmet as a bonus to be used in the full game - a perk that Team Ninja and Nioh fans will no doubt be familair with by now. Similarly, a survey will also be conducted in order to help facilitate feedback upon completion - Team Ninja really does pay attention to these, so I suggest you fill it in once you've given the demoa whirl.
The game is coming to Xbox Series X/S, PS5, Switch 2, and PC via both Steam and Xbox. The demo is available on all these platforms, too, and the final game will also come to Xbox Game Pass at launch.
To celebrate the announcement, the studio has released a new trailer (above) giving us an overview of the story, the key characters, and gameplay systems. This time, the battle moves on from the Yellow Turban Rebellion and the start of the Han Dynsaty conflicts, and moves into the Three Kingdoms era proper - the demo sees you join up with Liu Bei as he needles Cao Cao's defenses and tests the might of the legendary Wei Dynasty leader.
"Wo Long 2: Wings of Ember takes players to China in 208 AD, after the events of Wo Long: Fallen Dynasty, when the village of the protagonist and their friend, Pang Tong, is devastated by Cao Cao's forces as they march to invade Jing Province, plunging the land into war with demons roaming freely," reads a press release. "Seeking revenge, the protagonist will clear the way for Liu Bei in his fight against Cao Cao's forces, before joining Sun Quan in Jiangdong where they meet again with Pang Tong to devise a plan to repel Cao Cao as he sets his sights on the Red Cliffs.
"These two fledging talents, endowed with intelligence and courage, will soar through the skies above the decisive battle, taking on demons on the battlefield with an enhanced combat system. Players will rediscover the fast-paced combat of Wo Long, which combines attack and defence with evolved actions exclusive to this sequel. Using Insight Skills, they will be able to evade enemy attacks and use the terrain to their advantage to launch counterattacks, or even shift the momentum when outnumbered, making the fights even more acrobatic, exhilarating, and deadly than ever before."
I had chance to play the demo at Gamescom, and it's safe to say I'm impressed - I think Wo Long 2 acts as a sort of nexus point for everything Team Ninja has learned from working on Nioh, Ninja Gaiden, and Dead of Alive.

item.description:
The launch of Diablo 4's Season of Hell's Legacy got off to a rough start. The anticipated season was announced at BlizzCon over the weekend to arrive alongside a 30th anniversary celebration of the Diablo franchise. And though Season of Hell's Legacy eventually went live, it did so several hours after it was supposed to.
Players reported running into a number of login issues, with error codes 300006 and 300008 the most commonly reported. "We're aware of an issue preventing some players from accessing Diablo 4. The team is actively investigating and working to resolve the issue as quickly as possible," was the Diablo account's immediate response on X.
Two hours later, the Diablo account posted another update announcing the season launch delay, and Diablo 4 was entirely inaccessible throughout that period and for hours later. "We're continuing to address issues affecting today's launch of Season of Hell's Legacy. As a result, Season 15 is currently delayed. We appreciate your patience while we work to resolve the issues and we'll share updates as we have them."
It took another two hours for things to approve, with Blizzard confirming log in issues had been resolved, but some game features had to be temporarily disabled. The season ended up going live over six hours later.
Season of Hell's Legacy is the game's new live service season and a celebration of the Diablo series' 30th anniversary. It brings back Deckard Cain, an iconic character who's been in almost every Diablo game, to lead the player through a quest against all three prime evils: Baal, Mephisto and Diablo. The quest recreates several memorable moments from past games, and the season introduces nine Legacy Unique items inspired by their classic counterparts, plus myriad tweaks and alterations
The new season also coincided with the long-awaited launch of Diablo 4 on Switch 2, which means this outage was Switch 2 players' first experience of the game. Blizzard unveiled the new season at BlizzCon 2026 this past weekend, where it also announced the returning Amazon class from Diablo 2 for Diablo 4, coming in a paid pack in the first half of 2027, and where it surprise-announced Diablo 5, coming 2029, as well as a Netflix animated Diablo show.

item.description:
The original Wo Long is an overlooked gem. Fast-paced, brutal, and compelling, the game made a name for itself amongst hardcore action-RPG aficionados because of its key gimmick: that basically every single attack could be deflected. While some criticised this because it made the game 'repetitive', I thought it was interesting and well-executed enough to carry you through the entire playtime. Augmented by a momentum mechanic that rethought stamina for the fast-paced fights, and a still best-in-class 'morale' system that encouraged exploration and completionism, Wo Long has a permanent place on my harddrive.
And, after playing a good five hours of Wo Long 2, I can safely say it's better in practically every way. It's now my most anticipated game of 2027. The original game played it safe and stuck close to the solid foundations Team Ninja built with both Nioh and Nioh 2. The combat was grounded (or, as grounded as you're going to get in a fantasy game about Han Dynasty-era demons) and was clearly spun out of Nioh's obsession with bushido and the contrast between motion and stillness. Wo Long, as a series, was always supposed to be more concerned with Chinese martial arts. The second game is far more successful with this, mostly I believe because Team Ninja has the confidence to step away from those Nioh roots and experiment with more fluidity and verticality.
And why is that? It's because of Ninja Gaiden. Wo Long 2: Wings of Ember was in development alongside Ninja Gaiden 4, and you can tell. There's a "three-dimensionality" in this title that was lacking in the first game. In Wo Long, I would jump into most encounters, mostly because the slightly dopey AI wouldn't see or hear me coming, and I could land a fatal strike. It was an instant win. In Wo Long 2, though, you need to use your aerial attacks; it's baked into the entire combat system.
Maybe Team Ninja has internalised the criticism of the first game a lot, because whilst you can still deflect most attacks, even trash enemies have special moves that need to be dodged or countered, not just deflected. As a result, you need to get pretty dexterous with your hands, hitting the right combination of shoulder buttons and face buttons in some kind of unholy medley of Guitar Hero and Simon Says in order to survive even the most bog-standard enemy. Hey, it keeps you concentrating. Predictably, then, the learning curve is much steeper than in either the first Wo Long or Nioh, but the payoff is also more sublime.
For example, learning which attack animations leave your foes vulnerable to jumping moves before they are able to hurt you is important. Most enemies will glow red when winding up to attack you, and if you hit a shoulder button and jump on them at the same time, you will knock them out of the telegraph animation and inflict stamina damage. You need to be quick - and very close - in order to pull this off, but the rewards are worth it. You can also hold R1/RB and hit the deflect button for what is effectively a 'critical parry', which has a shorter effective window but does more stamina and health damage as a result. Basically, you use this when you've got the timing of your opponent's moves down to an art, finishing them off with a spectacular flair. Think Nioh 2's 'burst counter' but with more utility, and you're in the right area.
The level design is also more open (more akin to Nioh 3's semi-open world than anything else), and much more vertical than any other Team Ninja game I've played yet. This means exploration is more varied, with flags dotted around the landscape to tease you into encounters and light platforming challenges to capture them, that actually feel pretty good, given the genre. Movement all around has been improved on compared to that pervasive feeling of 'high gravity' in the first game. Whatever the other internal studios learned over on Ninja Gaiden 4 really is showing here.
So, we've covered my references to Nioh and Ninja Gaiden in the headline, but where on earth does Dead or Alive come from? It's the weapons. Each weapon has the unique moveset you'd expect from a character in a fighting game. That's always been the case in Team Ninja games, but it feels more distinct in Wo Long 2, possibly because of the aerial chains and combos that modify the base, ground-only attacks. Equipping straight sabres, spears, staves, glaives, hammers, or jointed flails, immediately makes you feel like you're embodying a different character from a fighting game roster. With various Martial Art skills - per weapon - that can be equipped on a whim, you've got more say over the final playstyle than you ever did in Ninja Gaiden 4, though I still miss the weapon variety and stance work of Nioh; I just don't think that system can be beat.
But in a game that's as singularly about forward momentum as Wo Long 2 is, six weapon classes is more than enough. You're not so much focused on picking holes in defenses as obliterating them entirely, learning the cadence of dodges, jumps, parries, and the level of aggression required per enemy in order to break down their guard and annihilate them. Jumping into a Martial Art move, twirling into a critical deflect, and then landing a fatal blow on an enemy causes pirouette like chain that makes you feel like the most lethal ballet dancer in China.
Wo Long: Fallen Dynasty was already a classic, in my eyes, weighed down only by whatever tendrils of influence Nioh still exerted over the breakout franchise. But, with Wings of Ember, Team Ninja is clearly emboldened and high on morale, confident enough to take all the slightly obscured gems of the first game and place them front and centre here. You can try it for yourself in a demo that is available on Steam, PlayStation and Xbox right now, too.

item.description:
Well this made me chuckle. After starting out with Two Point Hospital - a spiritual successor to developer Bullfrog Productions' classic sick-fixing sim Theme Hospital, Two Point Studios is now going even further into the past. Its newly announced Rides & Relics DLC for the excellent Two Point Museum is paying it back to Theme Hospital's much-loved predecessor, Theme Park - and you can even build your own coasters!
Two Point Studios actually has a direct link to Bullfrog Productions if you weren't aware: its founders, Mark Webley and Gary Carr, previously worked at the sadly long-defunct developer, and did, in fact, work on 1994's Theme Park. So there's a fun bit of symmetry going on here.
Anyway, Rides & Relics is the latest in Two Point Museum's run of largely excellent DLC expansions; those previous releases offering some neat shake-ups to the museum-running formula by introducing the likes of zoo animals, art appreciation, and even a spin on D&D-style tabletop fantasy. And, this time, the twist is theme parks and funfairs.
By sending your new Funfair Experts out to explore the new Gearbox Fairground expedition map, you'll uncover new blueprints and perks unlocking "17+" funfair-themed exhibits, including interactive displays and antique amusements (the trailer includes the likes of a pirate ship, haunted house, ferris wheel, popcorn stand, candyfloss stall, teacup ride and, um, cheese flume). It's also possible to build your own mini-coasters - adjusting height, tilt and camber - with talk of five unique coaster themes.
Additionally, Rides & Relics brings a brand-new museum location - Riquetti Gardens - alongside a new five-star campaign, new gift shop merchandise, and new themed items and decorations, including presumably theme-park-inspired variants for the helipad, ticket desk, benches, bins and more. Oh, and in order to keep visitors even more entertained, there are ten unlockable mascot outfits you can shove some of your poor museum staff in.
Two Point Museum's Rides & Relics DLC costs £9.99 and launches for Xbox Series X/S, PS5, and PC (via Steam and Epic) on 8th October. A Switch 2 release is "coming soon". Which just leaves one question: what are we doing next, Two Point Studios - cyberpunk or magic carpets?

item.title: Blizzard's decision to reveal far-away release dates for Diablo 5 (2029) and the new open-world StarCraft shooter (2030) at this year's BlizzCon represented an uncharacteristically transparent look at its future plans. So much so, there was a moment when the spotlight turned on World of Warcraft and it seemed we might get a monumental reveal there too. Read more
item.description:
Blizzard's decision to reveal far-away release dates for Diablo 5 (2029) and the new open-world StarCraft shooter (2030) at this year's BlizzCon represented an uncharacteristically transparent look at its future plans. So much so, there was a moment when the spotlight turned on World of Warcraft and it seemed we might get a monumental reveal there too.
Debatably, we did. Blizzard announced World of Warcraft: Forever, colloquially known as Classic Plus, a sort of alternate-reality take on the 2004/5 launch version of World of Warcraft - one that's expanded and remastered to provide a familiar but different experience. And that's a big deal: it's a notable moment in WoW's near 22-year history.
WoW: Forever reimagines the vanilla WoW experience with new zones, expanded original zones, new dungeons, new raids, new skill and talents, new race and class combinations, a new playable race - the Skyborne - a new battleground, and 100 new quests. There are new items and rewards, new things for professions, new reputation rewards, and account-wide perks. The graphics have also hugely improved, and there's an SD/HD character toggle to flick between the old and new looks while you play.
Perhaps more importantly, WoW: Forever is to evolve in different ways to vanilla WoW - it isn't beholden to the path the game originally took, unlike the previous Classic iterations of the game. "The future is untold," WoW executive producer Holly Longdale said on stage at BlizzCon. "We may see stories that could have happened, and some that didn't happen at all."
"One of the things that's singularly great about WoW is we have this game and this world and this design that has been continuously developed for the last 25 years," WoW: Forever principal designer Kris Zierhut said. "And we keep making it better. We made the graphics better, we made the rendering better, we made the lighting better; all that new stuff we showed on stage today.
"But we've also made the way the engine draws things move more efficiently. The way the server runs, handling players and moving them around, and all the things that handle spells and combat, all of that's been made more efficient and better over the years. We have this incredible engine and server infrastructure driving the game that is second to none. Why would you throw that away and start over?"
Modern WoW, too, is currently halfway through its Worldsoul Saga trilogy of expansion releases, with a huge upcoming titan battle teased at BlizzCon. That's a point Zierhut picked up on. "It's not like there's something wrong with [WoW's] story," he said. "We love the story. So going back to the beginning [with World of Warcraft: Forever], there's a chance to explore that story in new and different ways. So it's really hard to say, 'Well, what would a WoW 2 give you that World of Warcraft: Forever isn't already giving you?'"
Of course, making a sequel to a game like World of Warcraft - which was already large when it launched 22 years ago, but is colossal today - would be inordinately complicated and expensive. Blizzard has seen what happens when you force a migration within a player base in the bumpy transition from Overwatch 1 to Overwatch 2, and it would take years and years, and hundreds of millions of dollars to create something of the scale we'd expect from a WoW successor. In some ways, WoW's own phenomenal success has made following it impossible.
Plus, we've seen Blizzard attempt and fail to replicate it previously, when making sci-fi MMO Titan - a game that was eventually scrapped before being fortuitously salvaged into Overwatch, arguably for the better. Would Blizzard want to put itself through that again while making Diablo 5, a new StarCraft game, and while maintaining Overwatch, World of Warcraft, and HearthStone? With Blizzard owner Xbox preparing to cut 1600 more jobs and looking for areas to save money, I highly doubt it.

item.title: Valve is in the news again thanks to the impending launch of its Steam Frame VR headset. The developer recently opened up pre-order registration for the £889 / $1,059 standalone headset following months of wait. Read more
item.description:
Valve is in the news again thanks to the impending launch of its Steam Frame VR headset. The developer recently opened up pre-order registration for the £889 / $1,059 standalone headset following months of wait.
In a new IGN interview, Valve was asked whether the ongoing memory and storage crisis has had an effect on Valve's plans for the next Steam Deck. "Not really," said Valve developer Pierre-Loup Griffais.
"We've talked before about how we want to make sure there's a very delineated performance improvement for something like a future Steam Deck, I think we're still looking at it in the same way."
What Griffais is referring to is an idea Valve communicated a few times in the past: for a Steam Deck 2 to exist, it needs to offer a generational leap in performance. In 2023, the developer-publisher said that technology doesn't exist yet. Two years later, Valve said it had a "pretty good idea" of what the next Steam Deck might look like. In April, Valve outright confirmed it's working on a Steam Deck 2 and that the device builds on everything learned from developing the original as well as its hardware launches that followed.
With that in mind, Griffais explained Valve's goals with the Steam Deck 2 also haven't changed. "From what we're working on as far as the user experience goes and what the product that we're trying to build goes, it's very similar goals," Griffais said.
Steam Frame is the final hardware product to ship of the trio Valve announced last year, with the other two being Steam Controller and Steam Machine. The rising prices of Valve's hardware is partly what makes it difficult for Steam Frame VR headset - already a niche product - to make a compelling case for itself.
Despite being impressed with the hardware design and capabilities of the headset in Eurogamer's review of Steam Frame, Matt Wales said "Frame isn't a machine for high-end enthusiasts" and "doesn't offer a dramatically different in-headset experience to the far cheaper, more intuitive Quest 3".

item.description:
Let me paint a picture: it is day three of Gamescom; I have seen dozens of fantastic games, spoken to many enthusiastic developers. I am excited and energised by it all, but also at the point of slightly delirious fatigue (not helped by the Gamescom flu determinedly setting in). It is, in other words, a less than ideal time to be seeing a game as relentlessly, overwhelmingly intense as Alien Deathstorm. But play it I did - and half an hour later I found myself walking away thinking I might just have seen one of my favourite demos of the show.
Alien Deathstorm, as you might have suspected, is not a game with especially exotic ambitions. It's a sci-fi horror FPS built around dynamism, where emergent encounters impact the ebb and flow of its tense action with each playthrough. But foundationally, it's so singular in focus, so confident in its vision, everything you really need to know about it is right there in the title: it's got aliens (lots of them) and a cataclysmic deathstorm, and together, in just 30 minutes, they felt like they'd make my brain explode.
As for the set-up, you play as a Combat Engineer - a "highly trained" first responder - who's dispatched to a remote, off-world colony in order to figure out why everyone's stopped phoning home. Spoilers: it's because of the big bloody aliens and the big bloody deathstorm. Chuck in some beefy guns, and the whole thing sort of reminded me of a furious FPS spin on Dead Space - where a shopping list of stuff to fix keeps getting interrupted by all the sci-fi horror going on. Only there's no slow, anticipatory build-up of terror here; as it starts, you get a minute or two to acclimatise yourself, then it's just aliens, aliens, aliens swarming in from all sides. Developer Rebellion hasn't included a 'wipe visor' button for nothing.
As my demo begins, a voice rings out across the tannoy. They are Scottish, which pleases me. I'm urged to investigate the outpost's wonky reactor, which turns out to be the first of many systems that, inconveniently for me, have all decided to go spontaneously wrong. And even before we get to the shooty stuff, Alien Deathstorm is a wonderfully moody little number, all stark shadows and flickering industrial lights as the storm rages on: sand eddying through the air, shredded cloth flapping violently in the ceaseless wind, rain torrential, and great chunks of outpost debris skidding across water-slicked walkways and tumbling into the unknown.
It's a noisily intense opening few minutes as I brave the raging elements and chart a course for the outpost's "venting zone". And once inside, there's comparative calm. Ominous red light cuts through thick shadow, careless tangles of chunky cables snake in all directions along the floor, door mechanisms and bits of nonspecific machinery announce themselves with exactly the right kind of sci-fi thunk and whirr - but crucially, no aliens. I flip open a few crates, snag a blueprint and some credits, pocket a medical injector and a couple of grenades too. Then I find myself at the flame-spewing heart of the reactor's core, which I know because that's what the big on-screen overlay - with its cheekily Blade Runner-esque typeface - tells me.
I'm trying to paint an ambient picture for you now, because in about 30 seconds, after I've located a nearby terminal and downloaded some schematics, it all kicks off and the rest of my playthrough is a bit of a blur. Alien Deathstorm does not muck around, and I die several times in rapid succession as I try to find its chaotic rhythm. This is a game where threats - skittering ankle-high things with a propensity to hurl themselves at your face, huge hulking Predator-like things with viciously flailing arms - come screaming in from all sides, meaning survival depends on constant movement and momentum.
From here on out, I remember flashes of a prefab canteen, a snack machine gleaming cheerfully amid all the extraterrestrial gore. I remember finding a 'Remold' terminal for, I think, upgrades to my pistol, shotgun, and SMG. I remember an item station, where credits can buy new medical injectors, ammo, and grenades. And I remember heading out into a vast maze of cargo crates as rain slams against my visor, eventually finding my way underground - picking through the half-light among dangling wires and broken machines.
Somewhere in all of this I spy a lever, yank it and - behold! - yet more subsystems fail, yet more screeching arachnids come skittering in; their needly limbs lunging toward me as I continue to shoot, exploding in a shower of grue. And all the while I'm following a trail of dim lights snaking along the murky ground. Then another lever, more aliens, more levers, and still they come. Until soon, my entire world is lost in a blur of gunfire and bullets, a ceaseless soundscape of squealing things thudding against my brain. I die, I should say, a lot at this point, and I suddenly become aware of a Rebellion employee lingering over my shoulder, watching my endless deaths with a look of slight concern.
As my demo wraps up and I prepare to leave, he quickly steps in to reassure me, 'We'll have an easy mode in the full game'. And while my Alien Deathstorm demo is undoubtedly an absolute mind-melt of screaming murder and arterial violence, as I wobble shellshocked out the booth I think: I wouldn't have it any other way.

item.title: I knew going into BlizzCon 2026 that we'd get some Diablo news, but I expected a Diablo 4 expansion introducing a new Baal storyline, not Diablo 5. item.description:
I knew going into BlizzCon 2026 that we'd get some Diablo news, but I expected a Diablo 4 expansion introducing a new Baal storyline, not Diablo 5. It's a long way away, scheduled for a spring 2029 release, but that didn't stop Blizzard revealing enough information for us to build a picture of what the new action role-playing game will be like. And if there's one thing I took from the information, it's that Diablo 5 is much more than simply a continuation of Diablo 4.
The first sign was in Blizzard's confirmation that the game takes place a century after the events of Diablo 4, in a version of Sanctuary that has fully succumbed to evil. Diablo, the returning prime evil and lord of terror, has already conquered the world. Blizzard said it wanted to establish Diablo as a threat from the very beginning of the game, rather than being simply a boss you fight at the end.
In this apocalyptic Sanctuary, towns no longer exist. In fact, you can expect a more compact world (via IGN), unlike the sprawling open Eastern continent of Diablo 4. You are to constantly be on the move, travelling across the Western continent this time, in a caravan which expands in number the deeper into the game you get, and the more allies you encounter.
That was actually the idea of narrative director Jennifer Hepler (according to GamesRadar), the BioWare veteran whose name should be familiar to Dragon Age fans - she was a writer on Dragon Ages 1 through 3 (Inquisition). Hepler's idea was to bring elements from more story-based role-playing games into Diablo, with the caravan serving as essentially a roving campsite from Baldur's Gate or Dragon Age.
Companions are to be your vendors in Diablo 5, and each has their own story about surviving in a ruined Sanctuary - stories that play into the side quests they give. These characters include a Sister of the Sightless Eye - a member of a secretive order in the Western continent - but the most intriguing is, wait for it, a treasure goblin, the loot piñata of Diablo's world. Now, a treasure goblin has feelings, and Blizzard has said the character is "searching for meaning in a world where greed has lost its purpose".
Intriguingly, Diablo - the creature - reshapes the ruined overworld throughout the game. This manifests in a procedurally-generated landscape where topology, points of interest and roaming monsters change each time you visit it - as do the rewards. This is true for dungeons, too, which longtime fans will recognise as a core feature of Diablo 3, which didn't return in Diablo 4.
In another nod to Diablo 3, some of that game's classes are returning in Diablo 5, including the dual crossbow-wielding Demon Hunter and the martial artist, the Monk. Completely new in Diablo 5 is the Plague Knight, a heavily-armoured class who spreads disease across the battlefield and then consumes it for power, and Blizzard is aiming to have more Diablo 5 classes at launch than in any other game in the series.
The protagonist is described as the "Heir to Westmarch" and possesses a unique connection to Diablo, making them "both a threat and uniquely vulnerable to [Diablo]'s powerful influence", Blizzard said - how very Diablo. Westmarch itself has changed and expanded over the Western continent, a spread the game intends to explain as part of its story.
Itemisation in Diablo 5 is inspired by Diablo 2, apparently, which was another surprise given that the series' more complex systems were sanded down after Diablo 2, for subsequent entries. But Diablo 2's Runes and Runewords are confirmed as returning, and gear sets are also coming back.
Blizzard is going beyond that and "experimenting" with bringing back stat requirements for gear, too, meaning not everything you find is immediately equipable. Belts and item tiers return, and large items once again take more space in your inventory, meaning you'll have to manage your bags.These things combined could make for a more involved and deeper experience, one more akin to Path of Exile, and certainly more complex than Diablo 4.
The game's approach to multiplayer is less clear. Diablo 5 is playable solo and in co-op, we know, but beyond that, Blizzard is being coy. It won't yet say whether it's a shared world like Diablo 4 or if it's a fundamentally online experience. An evolution of Diablo 4's approach makes sense, but with town hubs seemingly replaced by an ever-present travelling caravan, where would players gather? Perhaps we're looking at something with fewer MMO-lite elements.
Combat changes remain the most mysterious, however, Blizzard only touched on them briefly in an interview with GameSpot, saying the team has "some great, interesting ideas about how to make combat feel even more visceral, even more action-forward", whatever that means. From the sound of it, combat in Diablo 5 is a straightforward continuation of Diablo 4, which was itself built on Diablo 3.
Diablo 5 is currently in full production and Blizzard is going to share more details about it in the coming years, and with the company apparently open to feedback, perhaps there's an opportunity to alter or help shape some of the features before the spring 2029 release.
Nevertheless, it's an exciting time for Diablo again, especially in light of a Netflix animated Diablo series being announced as well, and a Switch 2 version of Diablo 4. All that's left is to ask whether there's anything you're hoping to see in Diablo 5?

item.title: IO Interactive has announced it's pushing back the release of 007 First Light on Switch 2. The game's Switch 2 adaptation was expected to be released this summer, but has now been delayed to March 2027. Read more
item.description:
IO Interactive has announced it's pushing back the release of 007 First Light on Switch 2. The game's Switch 2 adaptation was expected to be released this summer, but has now been delayed to March 2027.
IOI said the extra time is being used to polish the game and optimise performance on Switch 2.
"We know many of you have been looking forward to experiencing Bond's reimagined origin story on Nintendo Switch 2, and we greatly appreciate your enthusiasm," IOI's announcement post on X read.
"To ensure we deliver the quality of experience players expect, we have made the decision to delay the release to March 2027, with the exact date to be communicated later. This additional time will go toward polishing the Nintendo Switch 2 performance of the game."
The news is especially surprising as 007 First Light was recently playable on Switch 2 at Gamescom. The studio is also taking the same demo to Tokyo Game Show this week, suggesting development was progressing smoothly.
But IOI never officially announced a release date beyond its intention to release the game sometime this summer. Then in late July, a 16th September release date popped up on Amazon Japan - a date that's one day from now.
"We were thrilled by the positive feedback on 007 First Light at Gamescom, and it's a great sign of the progress being made across the whole game as we head toward launch," IOI's statement went on. "We will share further updates as soon as we are ready. Thank you for your patience, understanding, and continued support."
007 First Light was released in May and has since sold more than 4 million copies across PC, PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. In Eurogamer's 007 First Light review, Rick Lane praised the game's emphasis on action and spectacle compared to IO's more cerebral Hitman series, and concluded that IOI was absolutely the right studio to create a modern James Bond game.

item.title: NetherRealm's next project has yet to be officially announced, but many believe it to be the third entry in the studio's superhero fighting game series Injustice. Now, there are new signs that select few outside the studio are playing Injustice 3. Read more
item.description:
NetherRealm's next project has yet to be officially announced, but many believe it to be the third entry in the studio's superhero fighting game series Injustice. Now, there are new signs that select few outside the studio are playing Injustice 3.
This all started with a post on Good Gamer Group, a company that provides NDA-protected testing services for game publishers. The post, since been deleted, was spotted by EventHubs (via Kotaku), which highlighted a number of curious pieces of evidence that all point to it being a NetherRealm project.
For starters, the listing includes two descriptors for the mystery game. It calls it a "triple-A fighting game" in one instance, and a "major 2D fighting game" in another. Neither is specifically limited to NetherRealm projects, of course, but as EventHubs points out, all the fighting games we know to be in the works are either smaller games or 3D fighters.
The location of the playtest is what gives us another clue. The playtest is held in Culver City, California, meaning the game is from an American studio. What's more, NetherRealm's parent company Warner Bros. Games also happens to be headquartered in the same city.
NetherRealm hasn't been shy about confirming it's working on new projects. Studio boss Ed Boon said in May the team is "actively pursuing another Mortal Kombat game" while "definitely doing more as well". As EvenHubs also points out, the studio has been hiring QA testers and designers at various points this year.
Even beyond the studio itself, two voice actors who were part of the first two Injustice games let slip in 2025 they're returning to voice their respective characters in Injustice 3, though they later walked it back, which is common when actors accidentally confirm the existence of unannounced projects. Indeed, Injustice 3 art popped up on a Warner Bros. Games artist's online resume back in April.
The timing of this playtest is another element pointing towards it being a NetherRealm game. Since the release of Mortal Kombat 1 in 2023, the studio has seemingly shifted to a four-year development cycle, seeing as that game came out four years after its predecessor, Mortal Kombat 11.
An Injustice 3 in 2027 would make sense, and a reveal at The Game Awards in December would also line up with the studio's reveal-to-release schedule. Mortal Kombat 11 was announced at The Game Awards, though the studio didn't do the same with Mortal Kombat 1. Whatever plans NetherRealm has for this one, we're clearly closer than ever now to some sort of reveal.

item.title: Rockstar Games hasn't said much about who's voicing the GTA 6 cast, but we now know at least one big-name actor attached to the upcoming crime epic: Stephen Root. Read more
item.description:
Rockstar Games hasn't said much about who's voicing the GTA 6 cast, but we now know at least one big-name actor attached to the upcoming crime epic: Stephen Root.
Internet sleuths have been scouring the web ever since the game's very first trailer, searching for even a whiff of the possible GTA 6 cast, and a recurring fan theory is now seemingly confirmed. Asked about the fan speculation by AP News, Stephen Root said, "Yeah, you're gonna see me in that."
You might recognise Root's face from his work in the Oscar-winning horror film Get Out and the Emmy-winning HBO series Barry, but his voice acting career is just as prolific. He has credits in everything from King of the Hill to Rick and Morty, and he even reprised his role as a bubble-loving yellow fish in the Finding Nemo video game.
"It's coming out November 19th, is the latest I know of," said Root. "But, I think, from the first roll out of GTA that they were doing maybe almost a year ago, they had my character in there and there were too many people who knew me from King of the Hill and my voice. So, I think that secret got divulged then."
Root didn't specify which character he's voicing, but fans have long speculated he might be playing Brian Heder. Straight from the horse's mouth, Rockstar's website explains that Brian's a "classic drug runner from the golden age of smuggling" who's "still moving product through his boat yard with his third wife, Lori." You can see Lucia and Jason going out for drinks with Brian and Lori in the GTA 6 extended look.
"I am so happy to be involved with it. It's an amazing thing to look at," added Root.
We'll likely hear more about the character as GTA 6's release date inches ever closer. For now, Rockstar's confirmed there won't be any generative-AI or microtransactions present in the game. GTA 6 is also running at 30 FPS at the moment, with the studio unsure about a possible 60 FPS option.

item.title: Marathon Season 3 and everything that was due to come alongside it has been delayed, including the sci-fi shooter's long-awaited full PvE mode. Bungie's next major update is now launching in December instead, and the famed studio is pivoting away from seasonal updates entirely. Read more
item.description:
Marathon Season 3 and everything that was due to come alongside it has been delayed, including the sci-fi shooter's long-awaited full PvE mode. Bungie's next major update is now launching in December instead, and the famed studio is pivoting away from seasonal updates entirely.
"We previously shared plans for Marathon's next major update to launch on September 22. We know many players were looking forward to it, and we appreciate your patience. We are adjusting our plans to ensure the update meets your expectations," Bungie wrote in a recent blog post. "The content originally planned for September will now arrive as part of our Symbiosis update on December 8."
December's Symbiosis update is promising a new Runner shell, the aforementioned permanent PvE mode, a social space where players can try out weapons together, improvements to the onboarding experience for newcomers, a "refreshed Perimeter zone" and an "experimental" team deathmatch mode.
Rather than a big seasonal feast next week, Marathon players can expect a slightly smaller update on 6 October that'll reset the game's progression and economy, while adding a new Rewards Pass and quality-of-life improvements. Vault Breaker, a different PvE mode that temporarily popped up a few months ago, will also return for a limited time.
From here, Bungie is done with the whole seasonal format, too: "We're also moving away from a strict seasonal schedule. Instead of tying major updates to fixed seasonal deadlines, we're giving the team more flexibility to build, test, and improve features before they are released.
"Since launch, you've told us Marathon needs more depth, more variety, stronger progression, and better reasons to keep playing over the long term. We agree. Addressing that feedback requires us to change both what we're building and how we deliver it," the studio continued.
Bungie's had a tough time both retaining existing Marathon players and courting new ones since the extraction shooter's launch earlier this year. Mass layoffs at the iconic developer - which saw at least 290 jobs cut - likely didn't help matters, either. Here's hoping the Symbiosis update can turn things around.

item.title: Valve has said its new Steam Frame VR headset, despite costing nearly £900 for a base model, is intended to "expand the market" of virtual reality headsets. That's both because it's lightweight and standalone, but also because it addresses a fundamental and long-running problem VR headsets have had. Read more
item.description:
Valve has said its new Steam Frame VR headset, despite costing nearly £900 for a base model, is intended to "expand the market" of virtual reality headsets. That's both because it's lightweight and standalone, but also because it addresses a fundamental and long-running problem VR headsets have had.
"For a long time, VR has turned itself into an accessory for your PC," Valve software engineer Jeremy Selan told Eurogamer in an interview ahead of Steam Frame's pricing announcement, "or in the case even of standalone, something that you have to decide to do first. Like, you might say, 'I want to play a non-VR game on my TV or on my PC,' or, 'I want to go try this specific VR experience.'" Regardless, it's an either-or situation - one or the other.
"From the outset of this product, we were really looking to do something new and to try to make customers not have to think if they wanted to do VR or non-VR games," Selan said. Therefore, a much bigger emphasis has been put on your ability to easily switch between VR and non-VR games - or movies or web browsing - while using the device.
"The non-VR experience is something that I use all the time," Selan went on, "and it's so comfortable because of the ergonomics of the controllers, the lightweightness of the device where you can carry it and use it in a bunch of rooms. So I find myself with this device for the first time putting it on, not even having decided what I'm going to play.
"I have the Steam catalogue in front of me - of course it's your computer and you can install non-Steam games - and I could just say, 'Am I [in the mood for] this non-VR game? Am I in the mood for this VR experience?' And you can sort of jump back and forth. And so this friction of 'am I going to bring out my VR device or not?': if you're already in it, the friction is zero. So I find myself playing a lot more VR and a lot more non-VR simply because of the intermingling of this device."
Matt picked up on this point in his Steam Frame review, and it's these aspects, coupled with its physical design, that make Steam Frame potentially a broader market device, according to Valve. "It's absolutely our goal to expand the market," Selans said.
Valve hardware engineer Joy Lyons added: "The idea here is that we want to have gamers be able to access more content through the Steam store and across all these different systems ... We see this as a product that's growing. This is obviously a great product for our PC VR users, and we love them and support them, this is for them, but we also see this as also a broadening of intent also for developers and then also for gamers just to have more access to more content and a really sort of premium experience in a VR headset."
Nevertheless, a base price of £889 for the 256GB Steam Frame model is a high hurdle to clear - a hurdle Valve's Steam Machine had to contend with earlier this year. The component shortage crisis is largely responsible for Steam Frame's delay from an early 2026 release. "We very much had to adjust the price targets and the volume targets and that's the reality," Selan said. "But we still believe at the current pricing it's a super compelling product. It's a great value. It's an amazing piece of hardware."
Joy Lyons added: "If all hardware is unaffordable then no one is able to enjoy or release or do anything. So, if anything, it's more important to be able to provide equipment that we're really excited about and we think moves forward the gaming experience."

item.title: After years of rumours, and 10 months since its official unveiling, Valve's long-awaited standalone VR headset, Steam Frame, is poised to begin shipping soon, and with a confirmed starting price of £889. Read more
item.description:
After years of rumours, and 10 months since its official unveiling, Valve's long-awaited standalone VR headset, Steam Frame, is poised to begin shipping soon, and with a confirmed starting price of £889.
Frame marks Valve's first VR headset since 2019's Index, and it represents a significant upgrade in almost every regard - from better screens and substantially reduced weight to movement and position tracking that's now handled on-device rather than external base stations.
Its improvements are perhaps less dramatic compared to more modern consumer VR headsets like Meta Quest 3, but they're still notable and you can find full specs on Valve's website. I've been playing with Frame for around two weeks at this point, incidentally, and you'll find more detailed impressions of the device in my Steam Frame review.
The most important bit of today's announcement, then, is probably the price, given Valve's has talked extensively about the tech before. And you'll be able to pick up a Frame with 256GB of storage for £889/€1,049/$1,059 USD (that's around £340 more than a 512GB Quest 3 for some vague comparison), while the 1TB model costs £1,089/€1,279/$1,299. Whichever version you opt for, you get the Steam Frame headset in the box, alongside the attached battery which lives round the back of your head, two controllers, a spacer, a charging cable, and a dongle - which is used for Frame's party trick: the ability to stream games directly from your PC with minimal fuss.
Frame is also being sold alongside a number of first- and third-party optional extras. A PSU from Valve costs £29/€39/$29, and there's an Ergonomic Accessories Kit that's an additional £59/€69/$59 and includes a headstrap, controller handstraps, handstrap battery doors, and an extended light blocker. Also confirmed is a £49/€59/$49 Accessory Replacement Kit, containing a replacement face gasket, head cushion, and light blocker. During an interview with Valve, word of an "enthusiast" accessories pack coming after launch also surfaced. It's said to include a "premium" audio solution and another swappable battery pack, but that's not something Valve's PR has confirmed.
As for Valve's official third-party partnerships, Zenni Optical is offering snap-in prescription lenses for around $67.95 a pair, and, if you're not happy with Frame's default monochrome passthrough camera, Arcturus has created a "truly plug-and-play" full-colour camera upgrade for £129/€157/$149.
Once that deadline has passed, Valve will do a "one-time randomisation" to determine reservation and waitlist order. When the process is complete, customers will receive an email on the 17th indicating whether they've made the reservation list or waitlist. Anyone who misses the initial sign-up deadline will automatically be added to the back of the waitlist and be notified once they're moved to the reservation queue.
As to when shipping starts, it's not entirely clear, but Valve says it expects to send the first batch of purchase emails out on 18th September, with more going out as additional units are ready to ship.
